subtopic: TRIBUTES TO DECEASED MEMBER FOR WATERLOO SOUTH

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO DECEASED MEMBER FOR WATERLOO SOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that hon. members were greatly saddened to learn over the week end of the untimely death of the hon. member for Waterloo South, Mr. Gordon Chaplin. In the brief two years that he was in this house his thoughtful, wise and mature approach to his responsibilities as a member and to the subjects that came before us in this house won for him the respect and friendship of members of all parties from all parts of the country.
Those of us who were privileged to remember his father when he too served Canada in the House of Commons were prepared to find in our late colleague the same fine qualities of quiet ability, friendliness and devotion to duty, and we were certainly not disappointed. His premature passing is a very great loss to his country, to his province, and certainly to this house.
On behalf of the government I would like to extend to his widow and his two sons our deepest and most sincere sympathy in their bereavement.

subtopic: TRIBUTES TO DECEASED MEMBER FOR WATERLOO SOUTH
speechtext:
I think this is the fourth occasion during this parliament on which we have been called to pay respect to the memory of colleagues who have departed this life during this relatively short period. We appreciate the references the Prime Minister has made this afternoon to our colleague. Many of us here and on all sides of the house have lost a friend, in some cases a very close friend, and all have lost a colleague who had won the confidence of hon. members.
Quiet, unassuming, a man of integrity, trusted and respected by all those who had the privilege of sitting with him, he had inherited and developed a position of preeminence in the business world of this country. As the Prime Minister has said, he was the inheritor of a proud political tradition, 20220-305
his father having been a member of a former government in this country and he himself having been a member of the legislature of Ontario for some years before he finally came to this house. His time here was altogether too short, and during the time he was here he was dogged by ill health. But he did take part in debates; he did take part in some committee discussion, and all those who had the privilege of hearing him or sitting with him realize the contribution he could have made had he been given more time.
We on this side have lost a friend and colleague. We appreciate the sentiments which were expressed by the Prime Minister. This parliament and the country are the poorer for his untimely passing, and to his widow and to the family we express our most sincere and deep sympathy.

subtopic: TRIBUTES TO DECEASED MEMBER FOR WATERLOO SOUTH
speechtext: The members of this party wish to join in expressing our profound regret at the passing of the late member for Waterloo South, Mr. Gordon Chaplin. Although he was here only a short time we all came to admire him for the sincere and conscientious discharge of his duties as a member of parliament. The members of this group wish to express our deep sympathy to his wife and his two sons, and to convey our regret to his colleagues in the Conservative party and to the people of the constituency of Waterloo South in the great loss they have sustained.

subtopic: TRIBUTES TO DECEASED MEMBER FOR WATERLOO SOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of the Ralliement Creditistes join their voices to those of their colleagues of the other parties to express their sympathy to the family of the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Chaplin) who departed suddenly. It is a loss for the Conservative party, the house and the whole country.
We all knew the hon. member for Waterloo South as an honest, sincere, generous and hard-working man. Some people will perhaps even say that he was daring, but it must be remembered that temerity, in the case of a soldier, is a virtue.
At this time we can say of Mr. Chaplin that we express, with deep regret, to his family and friends, as well as to the Conservative party, our sincere sympathy.
This also reminds us that even though we are in charge of the nation's business there is always just a certain number of days ahead of us and, whatever happens, we will have to meet, some day, the supreme parliament.
Once more we express our sympathy to Mrs. Chaplin, her two sons and the Conservative party. The official opposition lost a colleague, and the house a representative of the Canadian people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house has listened with a great deal of interest and approval to the announcement by the right hon. Prime Minister of the elevation of the former parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance to a position on the treasury benches as Minister of National Revenue. We noticed as we came in that his appointment had been made today, because we saw where he was sitting.
We on this side of the house want to congratulate him on this promotion, and possibly we should also congratulate him on the fact that he has perhaps escaped from the onerous task of being parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance and might find life, if not less arduous at least more interesting in the position in which he now finds himself. I think all departments of government have an impact upon individual Canadians, some more than others. For instance, citizenship and immigration, veterans affairs, health and welfare, all have a direct impact on many individuals; but speaking from some years of experience I think I can say that no department has a greater impact upon millions of Canadian than does the Department of National Revenue, to a greater or a lesser extent, sometimes to a very substantial extent, involving large sums of money. There are severe and heavy responsibilities placed on this minister. However, his professional

training and experience as well as the experience he has gained since he came here will assist him in this portfolio.
In addition, he will have the assistance of a large group of able civil servants on both sides of the family, customs and excise on the one side and taxation on the other, whose advice he will receive and will have to consider. All I can say, Mr. Speaker, is that during the years I occupied that portfolio I enjoyed it tremendously, and I am sure the hon. member will have the same experience. We congratulate him on his appointment and wish him well in his new role.

speechtext: No. From time to time the Post Office Department issues postage stamps publicizing primary industries such as mining, forestry, fishing and agriculture, which are of major significance in the economic life of the nation as a whole. The number of such subjects and of others which contribute to an awareness of our traditions, accomplishments and history, or foster a spirit of international good will and understanding, is such that it is not possible to honour in addition the specific products of our primary industries or of the hundreds of branches of these industries. subtopic: CONSERVATION OF AREAS AS ECOLOGICAL UNITS
CONSERVATION OF AREAS AS ECOLOGICAL UNITS
speechtext: What is the policy or policies of the present administration toward the conservation of the unspoiled areas of the country as ecological units?

subtopic: CONSERVATION OF AREAS AS ECOLOGICAL UNITS
speechtext:
The forest research branch is sympathetic toward the preservation and conservation of unspoiled samples of the natural landscape, and natural areas have been set aside at a number of forest experiment stations. Natural areas are defined as tracts of the native landscape, dedicated to the preservation of the endemic flora, fauna and terrain features for their intrinsic scientific, educational, aesthetic and cultural values. Exploitive activities that would destroy the values of natural areas are prohibited, and an attempt is made to exclude all disturbances caused by man and his works.
At the Petawawa forest experiment station, Ont., 17 natural areas taking in an area of about 500 acres have been set aside. At the Acadia forest experiment station, N.B., 12 natural area totalling 270 acres have been set aside. On the Riding Mountain, Manitoba, about 1,000 acres have been reserved in nine natural areas. At the present time, arrangements for larger ecological reserves in southeastern Manitoba and in the Prince Albert national park are being made.
In Ottawa the Department of Forestry is supporting the national capital commission in acquiring the Mer Bleue, an area of swampland and forest that will form an eight to 12 
square mile ecological reserve on the eastern side of the city.
The forest research branch has supported the acquisition of natural areas in the belief that they have two research uses: the study of specious and ecosystems as subjects of intrinsic scientific interest, and the study of how the twin goals of preservation and aesthetics in the native landscape can be attained and maintained.

speechtext:
Major capital grants, under the exhibition grants regulations, were suspended in June, 1962 and this suspension is still in effect. Annual grants including those for permanent improvements, judges' fees and junior activities are still available.
Consideration is being given to the reorientation of federal assistance to fairs and exhibitions from one essentially aimed at assistance for capital construction to one of augmenting the prize lists of fairs and exhibitions for certain classifications. subtopic: EXPROPRIATION OF LAND FOR GREEN
EXPROPRIATION OF LAND FOR GREEN
speechtext:
1.	Have the provisions of the National Capital Act in matters of expropriation of private property 
for green belt purposes ever been challenged in the courts and, if so, when and with what result?
2.	What is the real purpose of the green belt?
3.	What other uses does the national capital commission plan for expropriated green belt land?
Answer: 1. No.
2.	To control the location of growth of the urban population; to provide sites for parks, beaches, golf courses and other public recreational areas; to reserve land for government use in the future; to prevent urban sprawl and ribbon development along the main access highways, thereby providing attractive approaches to the capital; to utilize marginal farm lands for reforestation and conservation of wildlife; to protect land for continuing use as general and specialized farming and market gardening.
3.	Such other uses as may be approved by the governor in council from time to time.

subtopic: RESALE OF EXPROPRIATED LAND
RESALE OF EXPROPRIATED LAND
speechtext:
1.	What was the price paid for land in lots 26 and 27, Ottawa front 2 expropriated by the national capital commission on March 31, 1964 under expropriation order 319750?
2.	What profit was made by the national capital commission by subsequent resale of the major portion of this land?
3.	What profit has the national capital commission made since its inception by expropriating land from private citizens and subsequently reselling it?
4.	Is land expropriated from an individual and subsequently shown to have been expropriated unnecessarily, offered back first to the original owners at the price for which it was originally expropriated and, if not, for what reason?
Answer: 1. $8,750 plus $839.17 for assumption of liability to hydro, totalling $9,589 for 3.9 acres.
2.	Some 3.2 acres of the property expropriated by instrument No. 319750 were sold to the Ottawa public school board on May 10, 1960 as part of a block of land comprising 18.2 acres which was sold for $72,800. Thus, the cost in 1954 was about $2,575 per acre and the selling price in 1960, averages $4,000 per acre indicating a profit of about $1,525 per acre or a total of $4,880.
3.	Profits made by the national capital commission since February 8, 1959, for properties which have been expropriated and subsequently sold, amount to $310,272 for 48 parcels of land comprising 4,386 acres.
4.	The national capital commission requires the authority of the governor in council to carry out expropriations. It does not expropriate unnecessarily, although occasionally after an expropriation, plans change which

might require the disposal of property. Should this occur, immediately after expropriation, authority is sought for the government to return the property to the former owner by sale or abandonment, should the former owner wish to regain title to it. After it has held the property for a reasonable length of time adjacent urban developments generally preclude turning back the property to the former owners.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, pursuant to the understanding which we had late last Friday afternoon when we passed the resolution preceding this bill, when it was understood by the house that we would be able, on the first clause, to discuss matters of general

Importance in the same manner as we could had we the resolution before us, I shall speak for a very few moments-and I emphasize "a very few moments"-not because the matter to which I am going to draw the attention of the committee is unimportant but because I know there are other members of the committee who wish to speak on this matter. I do not want to take up too much time, so other members may be able to deal with this matter fairly quickly.
I am glad the Minister of Industry is in the chamber because I wish to refer particularly to the matter of industrial development, to which reference has been made from time to time, with particular reference to the province of Nova Scotia. This matter has been discussed at various times, and it was discussed particularly during the last election campaign. I am not going to take up the time of the committee by putting on the record lengthy statements which were made by hon. members opposite in connection with this matter, but I am going to give one or two short quotes. I hope that as a result we will have not only a discussion by hon. members on this side of the chamber but also by some on the other side including the Minister of Industry.
During the last election the then leader of the opposition, now the right hon. Prime Minister, said that a federal agency for the -development of economically backward areas would be created by this government. He also said that these areas would prosper with the rest of Canada if Liberal policies were carried into effect. He went on to say that a few parts of Canada would benefit especially, such as the maritime provinces, if this legislation were enacted.
The present government took over the treasury benches and various steps were taken. The Minister of Finance brought in certain incentive legislation to provide an impetus to the establishment of industry in the maritime provinces and other areas of Canada. I am not sure of the value of those incentives. This has yet to be proven, because the incentives will depend upon the co-opera-ration of the federal government, provincial governments and particularly private industry. It may be they will have some effect and purpose; it may be they will not.
We are now facing a situation in this committee where the minister who is responsible for the inauguration of these policies, the minister who is responsible for the development of these areas, made a statement in the house, or outside it, a short time ago with
Appropriation Bill
reference to certain contracts which were applicable to the maritime provinces and to Nova Scotia, saying that these would be terminated and the subject matter of the contracts would be transferred to other parts of Canada, and in one particular case to the province of Quebec. We have heard these ancient arguments-

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, did I understand the hon. member to say that I had made a statement in the house to the effect that this was going to be done?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext:
I am not sure whether the minister made the statement in the house, but he made a statement to the effect that certain contracts would not be renewed and that the basic work which had hitherto been carried out in this area would be transferred. In the case of one firm in Nova Scotia, Fairey Aviation, this work would hereafter be transferred to another part of Canada.
We in Nova Scotia have been rather surfeited with the ancient arguments as to why industry could not be established in the maritimes, and Nova Scotia in particular, to the effect that it was too far removed from the centre of Canada and that transportation costs are too high; therefore, unfortunately, it would be impossible to establish or maintain industries in the province because of the geographical factor.
This particular contract to which I have made reference has to do with equipment and material manufactured for anti-submarine work. It has to do with contracts which have heretofore been carried out by plants on the Atlantic seaboard, particularly the plant of Fairey Aviation Company on the Atlantic seaboard, which supply and furnish material for anti-submarine work on the Atlantic coast and in the Atlantic ocean. There is always the necessity for anti-submarine precautions on both coasts, but I think the members of this committee and the public generally would agree that there is a greater need for the development of anti-submarine projects on the Atlantic coast.
So there we have a plant which is efficient, which employs a large number of people, and which is producing material and equipment required at its very door. There can be no question of transportation costs there. There can be no question of being removed from the market. It seems to me very ironical, in fact it is the height of irony, that the minister responsible for the development of these great programs for these areas which they promised is the one who has stated that some of these contracts would be terminated.

Appropriation Bill
It is true that since then he has said in the house that this decision would be reconsidered, and that gives us some ground for optimism and for hope. For we know from our experience of this government that when a certain matter is reconsidered the policy is usually reversed and something else is developed, so we have some reason to think that having said they will reconsider the matter we will have these contracts reestablished on the Atlantic coast.
This is only one example of several which could be given, but I will not take the time of the committee by going into other areas. However, I should say by way of explanation that I am not suggesting for a moment that the province of Nova Scotia is necessarily one of the backward areas to which general references were made during the election campaign. When you read the record of what occurred last week in Nova Scotia and realize that the premier of the province took part in the inauguration of a huge refinery costing millions of dollars and in the opening of another fishery plant costing, I think, $10 million, you could hardly state that Nova Scotia was a backward area. But we do say that when this government was in opposition they promised the policy, a policy which appealed to the people, that they would inaugurate projects to assist that area. This particular industry-and this type of manufacturing has particular appeal-is centred in an area where all the advantages are in its favour, and we do not propose to have the old argument that it is away from the market and so on re-established or repeated.
In addition, we do not propose to have reestablished in other parts of Canada industries which have been established in our part of the country; industries which are successful, efficient and economic, and which should have the support of the government. The government of which I had the honour to be a member saw that the company to which I have referred received contracts in that area for development of anti-submarine work because it was a company particularly fitted to do this type of work, one which, as I said, had the market at its very door.
We have succeeded in establishing various industries in this region. A question was asked this afternoon-indeed several questions have been directed to the minister in this connection-regarding the establishment of an automobile plant somewhere in Canada. We blazed the trail and established an automobile plant in Nova Scotia; a great international company set up a plant there. We

hope the present government will be successful in establishing plants wherever they may deem advisable in other areas; but in this particular instance we are dealing, as I said, with an area which is particularly qualified to serve a particular industry, and we do not intend to stand idly by and see contracts which have been in Nova Scotia for some time and for which the firm concerned is especially fitted and suited transferred to other parts of the country, or to see the industrial life of Nova Scotia diminish at the expense of other parts of Canada.
That is why I am speaking briefly to this matter, and I speak briefly because I realize other hon. members have other matters with which they wish to deal. The minister may, if he likes, reply now, or he may wish to hear other references which will be made. With that I will leave this particular matter at this time because, as I said, there are other hon. members who may have something to say in connection with it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened with close attention to the remarks of the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, and I can assure you that what he has said regarding Nova Scotia in particular and the maritime provinces in general has my full support and, I am sure, the support of all members of the House of Commons who come from that part of Canada.
My constituency of Cumberland finds itself in a position not dissimilar to the constituency of Halifax with regard to cut-backs in defence work. I would also say that the situation in my constituency is not dissimilar to that of many areas in the maritimes. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings made mention of the statements of visiting politicians during the 1963 election campaign, and to the pie in the sky atmosphere they endeavoured to create in our area of Canada regarding the great and wonderful things which would be done if only a Liberal government were elected to office. Well, Mr. Chairman, I think the people of the maritime provinces have now had a taste of a Liberal government after watching one in action for a year, and after having seen a Conservative government in action for six years prior thereto. I am sure if given the opportunity they would far rather have the pie in the sky which was offered and contributed to by the Conservative government than the type of pie which has been provided by the present government during its short stint in office to date.

Not only that, Mr. Chairman, but it we go back beyond 1957-I do not want to take a great deal of time in going back to the 22 years of Liberal government this country was forced to put up with-I am sure many will recall statements made by Liberal speakers of the day who told us that while they could not attract industry to our area, they would assist us by establishing national defence projects which would give stability to our economy. Even though we would not be allowed to have the type of living which might be available to other areas of Canada, we would be provided either with a lower standard of living which we would get used to or we would be provided with a one way ticket out.
Now, unfortunately, we find ourselves in the position where another Liberal government is cutting back on the very thing which they once told us would form the base of our economy, namely defence establishments. Over the years a great many defence establishments have been located in the maritime provinces, and certainly they have provided a great deal of employment for the people. In many instances defence establishments were located in areas where other types of employment were not available and in many cases still are not available to the people. All of a sudden the government finds it is not able to balance the budget as it told the people of Canada it was going to do. It is not able to do a great many of the things that it told the people of Canada it was going to do. As a matter of fact, it is so hard pressed for money that it has started to cut back on the commitments made by the former Conservative administration with regard to national defence. In making these cut-backs it has not shown the consideration it should have for the maritime provinces as a particular area of Canada where chronic unemployment is a factor that must be given special consideration. It has proceeded to cut back and slash defence contracts, and thus throw people out of work in areas where they cannot just walk down the street to another plant and secure the employment they desire.
At the same time the province of Nova Scotia, as the hon. member for Digby-Anna-polis-Kings has stated, has been pushing forward and doing a tremendous job locating new industries. But it would be difficult indeed for the province to keep pace with the cutbacks and lay-offs that have taken place in Nova Scotia since this government took office. There must be a change of attitude on the part of this government or Nova Scotia,
Appropriation Bill
even with the enlightened leadership it is receiving from Premier Stanfield and the great industrial growth it is experiencing at the present time under his leadership, will still encounter tremendous difficulties because of the slashes now being made in a very unorthodox way by the present government.
I should like to deal specifically with what has happened in my area since the government took office, and compare the situation with what took place during the period we held office. In this regard I should like to quote from Hansard for May 5, 1964 at page 2963 when, during the period between 10 and 10.30, I raised this matter. I brought to the attention of the Minister of Industry the problems that were being created at Enamel and Heating Products aircraft division at Amherst as a result of the lack of overhaul and repair work from the Department of Defence Production. At that time the minister had this to say among other things:
Seeing this coming, the Department of Defence Production has encouraged aircraft overhaul orga-izations to seek production sharing work and has been prepared and has in fact provided considerable assistance to firms in securing contracts on a competitive basis with United States firms.
As the hon. member for Cumberland has pointed out, Enamel and Heating Products Limited have been more than usually successful in this particular regard. In this field they are one of the more enterprising and more successful companies. The Department of Defence Production has been concerned to see that the base from which they make their competitive bids in the United States will continue in operation, this base being provided by contracts from the Department of Defence Production for overhaul and repair of R.C.A.F. aircraft.
I am glad to be able to tell the hon. member that agreement has been reached with the company on what I think is a workable arrangement. a workable and practicable level of work which will enable them successfully to carry out the contracts in the United States.
I was very pleased with the statement made by the Minister of Industry in the house that evening. Indeed, I am not saying at this time that he is any less enthusiastic about keeping the word he gave me that evening than he was then. But I must say to him, and I am sure he will agree I am being fair, where is the work? Having had a good deal to do with the securing of contracts for this plant, I realize that you do not make a decision today and have it carried into effect tomorrow. That is not the way contracts of this nature develop. At the same time, however, that was May 5; we have almost reached the 1st of July, and the men who were laid off at that time are still unemployed. The company is still without the necessary work load to enable it to achieve

Appropriation Bill
the necessary production costs to honour its commitments so that the company will not face bankruptcy.
I do not know just where the matter stands now, but I do know that when I was home recently I found that the employees of that plant were in a great state of consternation as a result of the long lay-off which they had not anticipated once the minister's statement had been made. I found the union, which is endeavouring to negotiate a contract with the company at the present time, in a very difficult position with respect to its members. I have no doubt that the management of the company are in a most difficult position with regard to the union. How can the company negotiate a wage contract with its employees when it has no idea exactly where it is going to stand tomorrow or the next day or the day after? I also had my attention directed to a copy of a telegram which was sent to the minister and which reads as follows:
Following your pronouncement in the House of Commons on May 5/64 we received advice from your department as well as Canadair that steps were being taken to restore our defence activity to a work level and we passed this information on to the union to maintain excellent labour relations, but as a result of the long delay they are becoming quite restless and losing confidence in our promises.
Furthermore, acting on this promise we proceeded with negotiations with American contractors and have so far received additional American contracts for about a million dollars but due to the delay and the large loss we suffered in operations in May and so far this month we will have to take steps to abandon these contracts and lay off further men in order to husband our resources as well as effecting the economies in every direction including the cancellation of our participation in the Department of Trade and Commerce Glasgow fair and other foreign exhibitions. At the request of your department we have withheld giving information to newspapers and other government circles, but Fairey is evidently supplying newspapers with considerable inside information and in as much as Halifax is one of the most prosperous areas in the maritime provinces and receive the largest proportion of government expenditures we feel that the Halifax newspapers who advocate assistance to depressed areas are giving every good reason why the proposed contracts should be placed with us immediately even at the expense of Fairey because we are operating in a depressed area.
Certainly there is no good news for the minister in that telegram. There is certainly no good news for my area if this company should follow through with the allegations made in the telegram. It would be a dark day indeed for the county of Cumberland if the aircraft division of Enamel and Heating were to close down and throw out of work what remains of the usual work force of 265 people.

At the same time this plant, which has a rolling mill division in my constituency, suffered a great misfortune through fire last Wednesday, June 24. The result will be that another 200 employees will be out of work in my constituency. I do not know for how long they will be out of work. Certainly this is a substantial operation and has been a very successful one. There are a tremendous number of contracts, as the minister is aware, waiting to be filled. The damage to the equipment by fire will delay the filling of these contracts, and I do not know how long we will have to wait before the operation will be revitalized.
I should like to make a few more comments about the aircraft division which I hope will give the committee an understanding of the aggressiveness that was displayed by the management of this firm during the period we were in office, and even today. If I may refer back to the telegram from which I just quoted, mention is made of the fact that the company recently secured another $1 million worth of work from United States firms under the defence production sharing arrangement. I should like to quote some figures to give an idea how this firm has procured progressively a greater amount of work from United States firms, and what the result has been from the defence production point of view with regard to the aggressiveness they have shown.
In 1961-62 government contracts coming from the Department of Defence Production amounted to $1,540,000. This was coupled with defence production sharing contracts amounting to $223,000, making a total of $1,763,000 worth of contracts in the plant in that year. In 1962-63 the Department of Defence Production provided $1,500,000 worth of contracts for the plant and the company secured $165,000 in production sharing contracts from firms in the United States, for a total amount of $1,665,000. This was the last full year we were in office.
In 1963-64 the amount of work secured from the Department of Defence Production was cut from $1,500,000 to $575,000, almost by two thirds. However, the company managed to secure contracts from the United States amounting to $1,243,000, which gave them a total of $1,818,000 for that year. In 1964-65 they suffered still another cut in the amount of work available from the Department of Defence Production. The amount they received directly from the defence production department amounted to $384,000, but they managed to secure $1,305,000 from

United States firms, giving them a total of $1,689,000.
Now, if I may give the comparison of production sharing work on a percentage basis, I think we will have a still better indication of the aggressiveness displayed by the management. In 1961-62 it was about 13.5 per cent; in 1962-63 it was less than 10 per cent; in 1963-64, it was 68.5 per cent, and in 1964-65 it will be over 75 per cent. When you compare this with what is happening today you almost wonder if the plant management would not have been better to sit on their fannies and let the government feed them work rather than go out, as they have done, into the United States to obtain work so the plant could be kept in operation. In other words, every time the company secured a contract from the United States as a result of its own aggressiveness, work was taken away from it by the Department of Defence Production in Ottawa. This is not exactly the type of reward one would expect the plant management to receive for outstanding effort in securing work.
I noted in the Saturday edition of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, that one of the Halifax members indicated he was making application to the government in the hope that there might be a solution that would allow Fairey Aviation of Halifax to keep the Argus repair and maintenance contract and subcontract the work out to Enamel and Heating, thereby providing them with much needed work if they are not going to close their doors as a result of high production costs which would result in the cancelling of the contracts now on hand from the United States firms.
The hon. member is to be commended for coming forward with a solution that might provide employment both in his area and in mine. However, I should like to say this. I do not usually throw cold water on a suggestion of any hon. member which might benefit the economy of Nova Scotia. However, I found in my dealings with the Department of Defence Production during the time I was a supporter of the government that there was always a great deal of difficulty associated with subcontracts. Enamel and Heating have had subcontracts with Fairey Aviation in the past and they have not worked out so far as I am concerned. As a matter of fact, I took steps to try to have the work come forward from Ottawa as a firm contract rather than as a subcontract so that difficulties would not develop between the two firms.
Appropriation Bill
My view is that we in the maritime provinces need all the defence work we can possibly get. Far be it for one firm in the mari-times to be fighting with another firm in the maritimes about how much work either one of them has. I believe this situation develops when you have subcontracts of the type that must be awarded to these firms when either firm might be able to do some of the work.
Then one firm says "I should be doing that work" and the other firm says "No, according to my contract it is quite justifiable for me to do this part of the work; therefore I am going to do it." That is the only concern I might have with the possible solution put forward by one of the members for Halifax.
There is a lot of merit in what he is endeavouring to do, and a solution must be found because both areas of Nova Scotia are going to suffer substantially unless we are able to secure a work load for our defence and aircraft plants that will allow those people presently employed in the plants to continue working. Certainly I think members from the Halifax area would be most concerned in view of the fact that only recently the Blandford radar base was closed and a great many people were thrown out of work.
If they are to be faced with another lay-off on top of the problems they already have with regard to the shipyards and unemployment related to shipbuilding, mainly as a result of the cancellation of the all purpose frigate program, they must appreciate, as I do, that the economy of our area cannot stand the knockout punch it is receiving from one cut-back after another.
I would like to make a special appeal to the Minister of Labour, who is our Nova Scotia representative in the cabinet, to endeavour to get construction of the penal institution at Springhill started as quickly as possible. A great deal of needless delay has been associated with this project, mainly resulting from patronage, something which should never have entered into the matter. We are now a year behind the scheduled construction of that institution and we are still without a firm date for the beginning of construction, and this in an area that must have the sympathy not only of the Minister of Labour but of people in all areas of the country. I refer to the hard luck town of Spring-hill which is so valiantly fighting back from almost complete disaster. I hope the minister will get together with his colleagues in the cabinet to see to it that tenders for this institution are called early in July and that

Appropriation Bill
work is undertaken as quickly as possible thereafter.
I know there are other hon. members from Nova Scotia who wish to take part in this debate. I hope they will emphasize as clearly as possible that Nova Scotia cannot continue to see a government effecting cut-backs in almost every area of defence. The province is only able to continue because of the very aggressive leadership it is receiving from Premier Stanfield.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words on the general subject mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, and to touch on a few of the comments made by the hon. member for Cumberland.
There is no question but that because of the nature of scientific developments and the easing of tensions there have been some cutbacks in defence spending during the past two years. We in the Nova Scotia area, being adjacent to the sea, were in the position that a substantial portion of the amount of money spent on defence was expended in our area. A substantial portion continues to be spent there, and I was somewhat appalled to hear the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings suggest that the defence cut-backs were something new, something that had occurred only since the Liberals came into office.
I recall only too well that in years gone by, when the hon. gentleman sat on the treasury benches, he said that Camp Aider-shot, located in his own constituency, would never close so long as he was in the government, but in time the only sound of marching feet in the Aldershot area was that of the army of the unemployed. The changing needs of scientific warfare and of our national security will always be such that military expenditures and military bases will come and go with the changing techniques.
I think all of us on this side of the chamber would agree that government defence funds should not be spent for the sole purpose of charity. While we in the Halifax area felt it was extremely unfortunate that the radar station at Beaverbank had to close, I think no one in Beaverbank would suggest that the base should be kept open at government expense if it were serving no useful purpose to the security of our nation. It is true that we have had some cut-backs in the field of defence expenditures in Nova Scotia, but if one looks at the national percentage of defence cuts that have occurred as a result of the easing of tensions one will

find that we in Nova Scotia, percentagewise, had a very high allotment of defence spending in that area and we suffered a smaller percentage cut in expenditures than many other areas in Canada. Of course on the other hand, because so much of our economy is based on the defence industry it can be more severely affected by cuts.
One has to look at the over-all economic picture. Despite the defence cut-backs that may have occurred in the Nova Scotia area, today the unemployment level in the province of Nova Scotia is lower, and substantially lower, than it was at any time during the years of the Conservative government. That, I suggest, is an over-all test of the policies of the government. I think the area development agency and the Department of Industry in general have been looking very carefully at the needs of Nova Scotia, as well as those of other regions, and I have very high hopes for this department and believe it will result in great benefits to our area.
At the present time we do have an unusual situation in defence cuts, involving Fairey Aviation and Enamel Heating, and I am fully in sympathy with the aims of the hon. member for Cumberland in maintaining employment in the Amherst area as well as in the Halifax area. Enamel Heating, like Fairey Aviation, has been an efficient plant, a plant that greatly aided the economy of the province. Unfortunately the aircraft industry in Canada today is such that across the country bases dealing with the overhaul and repair of aircraft have had to make serious cuts in employment. Some of them have gone completely out of business, and I believe the over-all cut-back in the amount of work available has been in the vicinity of 45 per cent. Fortunately these cut-backs were not felt in Halifax prior to now, and I am confident that when the minister has ample and full opportunity to explore all the elements of the matter no cut-backs will occur at this time.
We are in this position; while we in Nova Scotia accept cuts in defence spending when they are necessary, that is when a program is being phased out or when a weapon is found to be obsolete, we feel it should be the policy of any government to spend as large a portion as possible of defence production funds in the maritime region, and that industries in the area connected with defence production should receive priority. Otherwise the whole idea of the program of the Atlantic development board and other such bodies would be meaningless. So, while we say we

accept cut-backs in defence, we cannot accept proposals to transfer defence expenditure out of the maritime region to other regions. What we have we hold, in the field of defence expenditure. This must be the case if the economy of the maritime region is to have an opportunity to develop and become less and less dependant on government spending. This must surely be our policy in the maritime provinces because of the necessity of making cuts in other areas of the defence field.
With regard to Fairey Aviation, I wish to say that this industry was established in Halifax by the previous Liberal government. It is an efficient industry with a wonderful record. It has provided a great deal of employment, and today continues to provide more employment than all the industries set up by Industrial Estates in Halifax, Kings and Colchester counties put together. I do not say this in order to belittle in any way the efforts of Industrial Estates, because it is a fine organization-

The hon. gentleman would like to have the exact figures. I will tell him that employment at Fairey Aviation is now in the vicinity of 750. While I cannot give him the exact figure for each of the small industries which have been established in those three counties, I suggest that if he takes the trouble to take the whole group and add up the numbers employed, he will find the result will not come to a larger number than 750 in those three countries. I would be very happy to hear from the hon. gentleman when he has done that.
As I was saying, Fairey Aviation has been a very important part of our economy, and
Appropriation Bill
we feel it must receive special consideration from the government accordingly. The Enamel Heating plant has an enviable record in the maritime provinces, and I want to say here and now that I am in a position, from conversations I have had, to know that contrary to the words of the hon. member from Cumberland, who seems to be expressing concern about employment at Enamel Heating a little late in the game, the Minister of Industry and Defence Production has been particularly concerned for some time about the problems of Enamel Heating and has been making every effort to find contracts for this plant at Amherst.
I would also say on the question of the Argus program, which has been discussed here today as it affects Fairey Aviation, that the company has itself shown every interest and desire to be of assistance in helping Enamel Heating. It is, perhaps, the problem of Enamel Heating which brings this question to the fore.
I wished to say these few words on the subject because I think it is a matter of great interest to Nova Scotia. While over the years we in this area have received a great amount of defence expenditure because of our geographical position on the coast, at this time, when some programs have had to be phased out, it is extremely important to us that no contracts should be transferred out of the maritime region. The partial transfer to Enamel Heating of some work from Fairey Aviation may be considered in a different light entirely.
But even as the United States government has followed the policy of attempting to spend government funds on defence production and other government programs in areas of lagging development, I suggest the same policy must surely be followed here in Canada; and I am confident that this government, which has done so much already for the Atlantic region, as exemplified by funding the Atlantic development board with $100 million as well as by other similar provisions, will show the same concern in the matters now under consideration. I am sure the action of the Minister of Industry and Defence Production in carrying out a full and lengthy investigation into this whole problem shows his concern and his willingness to try to work out some policy which will be equitable for us and result in satisfaction for all.

speechtext:
There are those who take that view. I wish the silent member over there who never gets to his teet would not interrupt me. There are those who say we are obstructing business when we speak in this house. However, this is a subject of serious import, and those who are affected by it would not consider my intervention as obstruction. I might refer to the hon. member for Halifax-how am I to distinguish him; the one with the least hair?-who mentioned the closing of defence establishments and was shocked, he said, to hear that the member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings had had something to say about it. Camp Aldershot had closed, and so on; the former minister, my hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis-Kings had said it would not close.
Well, for the information of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan), a former minister of national defence-I think his name was Campney; he went out of the house in 1957- announced the intention to close Aldershot, but it was continued for some time after that. This was when the great movement was on to Gagetown. I think the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan), was as far at sea with regard to that as he was with regard to some of the other matters he mentioned. He said, somewhat vehemently, "What we have, we hold". I understand that he is now, along with other members from Nova Scotia, making an attempt to hold some of the things which came to Nova Scotia during the period 19571963.
I should like to say something now about the ferry service at North Sydney. On March 14 there was a board of trade meeting at North Sydney, and an annual dinner. The chief entertainment for the evening was provided by the Minister of Transport, who was the guest speaker. Incidentally, I hope he is feeling much better. I regret he is not in his place today. I understand he is quite sick. I hope it will not be long before he is back again and in a position to read the remarks I am making now, and provide us with some sort of answer. At that annual dinner the food was good, but the entertainment was not very good. On that occasion the minister announced that there would be a ferry operating between Argentia and North Sydney. This was one of the projects for which money had been put in the estimates by the previous administration; it was also one that had been announced by the former minister of transport during the latter part of last year, before he was

demoted. Then the Minister of Transport went to North Sydney and reannounced it. Plans for this project had been under way for many months. The unique part of his remarks are reported in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald. of March 16, the Monday edition, and I should like to quote from that newspaper:
Mr. Pickers^ill, now in Newfoundland, told the Chronicle-Herald after the meeting that the proposed third ferry would take on loaded box cars and have them unloaded at Port aux Basques.
The announcement appeared to have caught off guard some 200 persons at the North Sydney board of trade meeting.
Under the proposed new arrangement, trucks, as well as railway cars, will be unloaded at Port aux Basques, instead of at North Sydney. For shipment on the existing ferry, William Carson, goods are unloaded from the cars.
So under this program it would appear that the new ferry would take loaded railway freight cars aboard the vessel at North Sydney and they would be shipped loaded to Newfoundland. On March 23 I posed a question on this matter to the minister. As usual he was quite evasive; I have not been able to get any information from him. At that time he stated that freight was increasing every year through these ports and as a result there was increased work. This is quite true; freight is increasing annually and I hope it continues to increase. But should a system of this nature be put into effect, very little work will be available in North Sydney, as far as freight handling is concerned. To enlighten the committee a little more on this matter I would like to quote from the Cape Breton Post of March 16, in which there was a story as follows:
While hon. Mr. Pickersgill did not elaborate on or outline details of the new ferry for the North Sydney-Port aux Basques run, it is understood here that it will be in the form of a car-freight ferry, one which would transport loaded freight cars from here to Port aux Basques.
These cars, it is reported, are ones that would arrive here loaded, and then be placed aboard the ship as are.
So we go on, and we find that this situation has been causing a great deal of anxiety among many people in Cape Breton, boards of trade, members of town councils, unions, and so on. The Cape Breton Post of June 5 carried a report of a meeting of the board of trade at North Sydney. The article is entitled "Transshipping of freight hit", and it says:
-in the event of transshipment handling of freight at Port aux Basques could "in time deal a pretty vital blow to the labour picture of North Sydney".
This was a statement made by the president of the board of trade. Then there was a

meeting of the town council in Sydney Mines at which the secretary of the union, local 1259, I.L.A., appeared and presented his case. He asked for support. Then I understand the representative from the union approached the Minister of Labour on the subject, and the following appears in an article in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, of June 12. The article is headed, "Some facts first-meeting later":
William Quirk, recording secretary of local 1259, I.L.A., sent a letter to Mr. MacEachen stating that the local's membership was "greatly disturbed" by the "persistence of strong rumours and some solid facts" that create a strong impression of impending disaster to the union and town of North Sydney.
The Minister of Labour reported to the newspaper concerned in Halifax that he felt this was one of the questions raised last fall when a delegation met with him and other ministers concerned with regard to the shipment of freight through the port of North Sydney. At that time he said the concern expressed was somewhat exaggerated and he would look into the situation as it then existed. In their letter to the minister the longshoremen said it was their understanding that a special tariff was issued to provide through rates to inland ports in Newfoundland that would make the service highly competitive with the C.N.R. This is a separate item altogether from the proposed new ferry. They went on to say that what was even more disturbing was an agreement that had been made between the C.N.R. and C.S.L.-Clarke Terra Nova services, giving the latter the privileges of transporting from Montreal all the freight shipments originating in Ontario and a large part of Quebec that were not specifically marked "via C.N.R.". The association asked the Minister of Labour for his assurance that their fears were groundless or that definite steps would be taken to provide an immediate equal opportunity for alternate employment for this group. Those are two very important items, Mr. Chairman, about which I wish some information, with regard to the construction of this ferry. We want to know whether any arrangement has been made whereby competition is provided with the help of government incentives which work to the detriment of the port of North Sydney.
Here again there is an article in the Cape Breton Post with regard to the joint meeting of the two town councils of North Sydney and Sydney Mines. Another item in the Cape Breton Post of June 13 is headed, "MacEachen optimistic". Since my very good eol-
Appropriation Bill
league from Cape Breton is an eligible bachelor, I am glad he is still optimistic; but this would appear to refer to something else:
Mr. MacEachen said the elimination of freight handling jobs would depend on the growth of traffic business and, with the possibility of increased traffic, would mean increased employment through the years.
That is quite true, provided we are not going to have the type of ferry that has been suggested. All we want is an explanatory statement from the Minister of Transport or the Minister of Labour with regard to the type of ferry that will be operated on this service. On another occasion the Minister of Transport said, "The hon. member knows"- referring to myself-"that this is two or three years in the future, and there will be plenty of time to look into the matter of employment." I say that now is the time to look into the matter, not two or three years from now, because employment will have been eliminated in North Sydney by that time. The minister should investigate the situation immediately, make some statement on behalf of the government, and thereby alleviate all the worry that is being caused to the people of the port of North Sydney, the town of Sydney Mines and the surrounding areas from which men come to work at the port. In another article in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of June 13 it is reported that the Minister of Labour said he felt the volume of freight traffic through North Sydney would increase in the future. We have heard this story all the time, that freight is going to increase. That is good; I like to hear it. But I do not like to hear that we are perhaps going to have a freight ferry that will take loaded railway freight cars from the port of North Sydney and they will be unloaded at Port aux Basques, in Newfoundland rather than in Nova Scotia, and the handling will be done in Newfoundland. At one time I asked the Minister of Transport whether this meant the standardization of the railway in Newfoundland, and he said, "Definitely not". I could not draw that conclusion; the only conclusion I can draw is that there will possibly be a yard set up at Port aux Basques with narrow gauge tracks and the freight will be transferred from the standard gauge to the narrow gauge tracks for distribution throughout Newfoundland at Port aux Basques.
Another meeting was called for the purpose of organizing a port commission, which all the interested parties of the area attended. According to the Cape Breton Post for June 16, 1964:

Appropriation Bill
Mayor Hartigan In his opening remarks referred to the interest and concern of Sydney Mines in the local labour picture at the C.N.R.'s terminus, due to the fact that many Sydney Mines people were working here.
He also stressed the very great importance of a "united front and effort" if any move to combat possible setbacks are to be counteracted successfully. "We should not," he said, "under any consideration or circumstances make any kind of political issue or football out of this situation".
I can understand why the mayor would make a statement like that. He is a non-political person and does not take part in politics, although I must state he is past provincial president of the Nova Scotia Liberal association; but I am sure his heart is in the right place and that he is willing and anxious to do anything he can to assist in this problem.
A few days ago I posed another question to the minister about this matter and again got no reply. I see the Minister of Labour with us today and I should like to ask whether he is in a position to provide some clarification so as to clear up any misunderstanding about this. I trust that anything we have heard is only rumour and that freight will always be handled at North Sydney. Another point I should like clarified, one with which he is familiar because we met on several occasions in this regard, concerns the possibility of another steamship line receiving certain preferences, priorities or incentives to assist the taking of freight away from North Sydney, thus causing more unemployment and further competition for the C.N.R.
Another point concerns increased employment, and this question was mentioned by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan). We are all pleased to hear about this increase, but may I quote to him a statement issued by the Minister of Labour on Monday, April 20, which appeared in the Cape Breton Post. The minister said at that time:
Since 1961, the labour market on Cape Breton island has improved, and there has been a consistent increase in employment in the service industries and in the manufacturing of steel, pulp and aluminum products.
That was in 1961, and if I recall correctly the present administration was not in office at that time.
Before going on to something else, Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer to certain areas facing cut-backs, reductions in force, and so on. This matter concerns a number of ministers. I am sorry the minister of northern affairs is not here. He was here a moment ago and perhaps he is behind the curtains and will hear me. There has been a very

considerably reduced work program in the Cape Breton highlands national park, and much remains to be done. This park provides employment for the many people deserving of that employment. Incidentally, I suggest the works program at the park in the past year has been the lowest for quite a number of years. I am receiving representations from many people in the area who are looking for employment of some type. They are not in a very good way financially. I am pleased to say that I made representations to the Minister of Labour on their behalf and I hope and trust he is doing his best to find employment for them. I have received letters from the clergy in the area, who have advised me there are people in destitute circumstances in Victoria county. If more work were provided in the Cape Breton highlands park this would fill the bill somehow.
Another matter I should like to raise with the minister of northern affairs is this. I should like to know whether he can advise the committee whether the Liberal councillor at South Ingonish is the hiring agent now for the park. I am curious about this. The information I have received suggests that the Liberal councillor in South Ingonish beach provides the names of people who would like employment to the superintendent of the park, and the superintendent in turn telephones the national employment office and informs them whom he wants.

I hear an interjection from the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan), who asks whether I made the appointments. When we were in government I was pleased to play some part in placing men in work there. Mr. Chairman, I would like to speak briefly this afternoon on the situation of farmers in the province of Quebec.
You know that, last week, nearly 10,000 farmers marched on the capital of the province of Quebec.
This march was intended to force the population, and especially the provincial government, to realize the situation of the Quebec farmer faced with constantly rising land taxes in that province, to which farmers have to contribute more and more, and also to force the population to realize the fate of the farmer in that province.
When the Liberal government came into office in Ottawa we were entitled to expect, particularly after the great promises which had been made during the campaign, that this government, during its famous first 60 days, would find a magic formula to solve the problems of Quebec farmers. Unfortunately, during the 14 or 15 months the present government has been in power, not only has the position of the Quebec farmer not improved, but it has deteriorated from day to day, not only because of events, of trade in general, or of the market situation, but also because of the attitude taken by the present government.
It should be kept in mind that under the present government, the situation of the dairy industry in Quebec, far from improving, is worsening. Instead of meeting the wishes of our farmers, the government abolished the 30-cent subsidy per cwt. of milk delivered to cheese factories. It also abolished the 25cent subsidy per cwt. of milk delivered to butter factories. It is reported that all this will save from $6 to $8 million.
I realize that the government must save money, but why must it always be at the expense of farmers? It is against this that we are protesting.
It must be borne in mind too that the government has also reduced the 12-cent subsidy on butter granted by the previous government in order to dispose of butter supplies

and, at the same time, to maintain the subsidies paid to farmers, especially milk producers of the province of Quebec.
The government failed to appreciate the situation. It failed to realize that the expenses of our farmers increase constantly and that their income, instead of increasing proportionately, remains the same or is decreasing.
In this morning's issue of Le Devoir, there is an excellent editorial by Mr. Claude Ryan, in which he explains very clearly the situation of eastern farmers whose purchasing power is decreasing. According to Mr. Ryan:
All surveys indicate that the purchasing power of the farmer has been constantly decreasing for 20 years. The farmer is now earning a few dollars more than previously, but this increase of the gross income is insufficient to meet the increase of the cost of necessary services and equipment.
The present government refused to face the facts. It is true that during the election campaign, we heard about the famous department of agriculture for eastern Canada which was supposed to solve all our problems. This department was a magic formula and worries were to disappear. This government has been in power for 15 months and we are still waiting for a department of agriculture for eastern Canada which is supposed to be a magic formula to remove every evil and smooth out the difficulties of our farmers.
There is of course the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) who is partly responsible for ARDA and the redevelopment of our rural areas. It is a long term plan but up to now, in view of the relations between the Minister of Agriculture of the province of Quebec and the Minister of Forestry, it is obvious that the efforts of the new minister are not particularly welcomed by the Quebec farmers, especially when one hears a Liberal minister, such as the hon. Mr. Courcy, who makes no bones about appearing on T.V. to give a good scolding to the federal minister responsible for rural development. It was an unusual sight, but there must be some grounds to warrant such a situation. Is it the reason why the minister of rural development has felt it necessary to go on holidays in Italy for a rest?
I do not know, but, in any case, when the minister is no longer contemplating long trips around the world, I hope he may find the time to consider the problems of the Quebec farmers.
One day, I was visiting the rural area of my constituency of Three Rivers, which has many farming communities, and I was talking to a farmer whose family had tilled the same
Appropriation Bill
land for nearly 200 years. He was an old gentleman, very much respected in the parish, and the owner of beautiful farm land which can be advantageously compared to any in the province of Quebec. This old gentleman said to me: Mr. Balcer, you, the politicians, will definitely have to do something. I asked him: Why? And he answered: Listen, my family has been on this farm for almost two centuries, and today, when everybody says that there is prosperity in the whole western world, when we are told that in Montreal, 50 storey skyscrapers have been built as well as tremendous speedways, at this very moment, for the first time in seven or eight generations on the same farm, my family will have to leave the land which has fed our forefathers for the last 200 years.
And he explained why. He told me that he had two sons working on his farm, who were excellent farmers, and laboured from daybreak to sunset; but unfortunately, all the father could give them for their petty expenses was $5 or $10 a week, while, just beside them, lived two boys who, though not exactly hard workers, had found positions in a Shawinigan Falls plant, where they earned a salary of $100 a week working from eight in the morning until five in the afternoon. They were coming back to the village with a shiny new car and dated the prettiest girls in the community, because they had a car, and so on.
Now, the old gentleman told me: Would you tell me, Mr. Balcer, why our two boys would want to remain on the farm and keep up an age old tradition?
This problem recurs throughout the province and throughout all eastern Canada. With that problem to face, the government does not assume its responsibilities, but takes the following attitude: The eastern farmers' problem will always remain a problem, let us be satisfied with the status quo.
Now, we are speaking about an important class of our society, which gives outstanding service to the country as a whole. This is a category of people with old traditions which have their roots in this country's history, and these people should not be abandoned and left to their fate.
At all costs, the government must come to a decision with regard to feed grains for the eastern farmers. This is a question the government must solve. It must build warehouses in the east, in our harbours on the St. Lawrence river; it must also pay for the transportation, from the west to the east, of such feed grain, and also for storage. In

Appropriation Bill
addition the government must establish a board which will look after the purchasing of feed grain and see to it that there is no undue speculation detrimental to our farmers. All that must be done.
A crop insurance scheme for our farmers must be initiated. Stabilization of farm prices must also be achieved. But mainly the government must find new markets. The government is not looking for any outlets for our eastern farmers. The problem must be tackled with vigour, because the situation is much more serious than we think.
When we consider that 10,000 farmers marched as a group to Quebec in order to lodge a protest with the government, I say to this government that, before long, those thousands of farmers will gather in front of the parliament in Ottawa, if the government continues its easy-going and forsaking policy regarding eastern farmers.

Let us be men of goodwill, instead of men of ill-will or no will at all. We will then save, not only Canada and confederation, but the human being who works for the development of his country.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to take this opportunity to make some brief remarks on the interim supply bill that is before us, but I wish to speak on a different subject. It arises from a question I directed to the Minister of Labour asking whether the Gill report on unemployment insurance would be debated during this session. He replied that if parliamentary time permitted this was one of the matters which might be dealt with during the session. Mr. Chairman, the Gill report was presented to parliament in November 1962. A couple of months later there was an election, following which there was a change in government. During the time the present government has been in office there has been ample opportunity to bring in the Gill report on unemployment insurance, but nothing has been done. Not only that, but we have still not had word from the Minister of Labour as to when the matter will be debated in the house.
My interest in the report and the recommendations is well known to the house, particularly that part of it which deals with unemployment insurance for the farm labourer. Not very long ago I presented a bill to the house which was talked out, which does not mean that there is no justification for bringing farm labour under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I should like to put on record a report from the national employment service, which reads as follows:
The present shortage of good farm labour on the prairies appears to he more serious now than at any time in the past 10 years, says the April monthly report of the national employment service.
The N.E.S. also said the number of transient workers available in 1964 is much lower than it was at the same time one year ago. The number of these workers has been seriously depleted through heavy recruiting of workers for jobs in various mining operations on the prairies.
In Manitoba, the N.E.S. offices report they cannot keep up with the demand for good farm workers. There is a serious shortage of couples for dairy farms and farm machinery operators anticipated, the report said.
A number of farm organizations have suggested that training programs be established to educate prospective farm labourers in handling and maintaining farm machinery.

Not so long ago there took place a meeting in Winnipeg, as a result of which the unemployment insurance fund will be asked to include farm hands under the benefits of the Unemployment Insurance Act. According to the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix this recommendation was made:
Winding up a two-day meeting in Winnipeg Wednesday, the prairie regional employment committee recommended that unemployment insurance coverage be extended to include farm labourers. "Farm labourers should be entitled to the same benefits as city construction workers", F. C. Cron-kite of Saskatoon, chairman of the 15-man committee said, commenting on the resolution.
The reason I have placed bills and motions on the order paper in the past is due to the serious situation which has developed in the agriculture industry of this country. The Gill report says that insurance for farm labourers is not easily provided, but I submit that the report should be presented and the recommendations discussed. What annoys me most is this, that in the dying days of 1957 the then Liberal government provided unemployment insurance for self-employed fishermen. I am not going to stand up here and say that these self-employed fishermen should not receive assistance; but the point I do make is that if the former minister of fisheries, Mr. Sinclair, who represented a constituency on the west coast, as well, I am sure, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, were instrumental in bringing about this change in the Unemployment Insurance Act, I am puzzled why the ministers in the cabinet who come from the prairies have not demanded that farm labour should also be included under the Unemployment Insurance Act. As a result of this omission the farmers both in the east and west have suffered and lost money because they cannot get insurance coverage for farm labour. If the Unemployment Insurance Act can be applied to self-employed fishermen it is certainly much easier to apply it to farm labour.
I should like to read what was said in the Gill report about implementing unemployment insurance for fishermen. I refer to paragraph 26, page 110:
One area of existing coverage where an employer-employee relationship does not in fact exist is that relating to the coverage of self-employed fishermen. This question is discussed subsequently in this chapter: consequently it will be sufficient here to state our view that this group should not be covered by the unemployment insurance plan that we are recommending. We recognize that there are many economic and social problems in connection with fishermen and the fishing industry in general-

-but they are not being satisfactorily solved, in our view, by the attempt to make the existing unemployment insurance plan apply. Indeed, this attempt is leading to difficulties and distortions within the fishing industry and in the application of the plan to other groups.
So apparently they felt the plan was not satisfactorily workable as far as farm labour was concerned.
In 1956 some coverage was extended to those in agriculture who were concerned with the raising of poultry and egg grading, and the raising of race horses, saddle horses or light harness horses; but according to the Gill report the commission found it difficult to administer unemployment insurance for farm labour. According to paragraph 20 on page 108 they state:
We recommend that the general principle be followed of extending coverage as broadly as possible so long as the necessary administrative procedures may be carried out to see to it that the rules of the plan are adhered to in a satisfactory fashion.
If unemployment insurance can be administered in the case of self-employed fishermen, I cannot see that there should be any difficulty in extending unemployment insurance to farm labourers.
The Gill report has been before parliament for the last two years and nothing has been done. I remember well that at the time the commission was appointed it was said: All we need is the Gill report and as soon as the Gill commission's recommendations are made steps will be taken. How long do we have to wait before the Gill report comes before the house for debate and discussion? The report contains valuable information as well as valuable recommendations. Although in some areas the recommendations as far as farm labour is concerned may not be to my satisfaction, nevertheless ways and means can be found whereby unemployment insurance can be made to apply to farm labour.
I took this opportunity to speak on interim supply. As I said, I have brought several bills before the house on this matter but they have been talked out. One reason for opposing them that has been put forward is that the Gill recommendations have never been presented to the house and that until the report is debated and discussed in the house no steps can be undertaken.
I think there is an urgent necessity for this report to be debated. As I indicated, there is a big shortage of farm labour on the

prairies at the present time. When our farm organizations recommended that training programs should be implemented to teach men how to operate machinery, I think it is time for the government to take this matter into its hands and see that unemployment insurance for farm labourers is provided in order to help to deal with this problem.
I have met many farm labourers, and these men prefer farm work, but they have to try to get other types of work because if they work on farms they cannot receive unemployment insurance when the work ends. I am sure that if unemployment insurance were extended to them the problem not only of the west but all over Canada will be solved, to the extent that some of these labourers will be available to work on the farms all year round.
As I have done on many other occasions, once again I urge the Minister of Labour to give serious consideration to having the Gill report on unemployment insurance brought before the house for discussion, so that steps can be taken in this regard because, as I have said, the problem is a serious one and the longer it continues the worse it will get.
