subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, from the remarks that have been made by the hon. member for Greenwood and other hon. mem-

bers who have spoken on this very important bill the impression seems to have been left that the committee on defence approved of the bill completely. It is true that technically it was passed without any amendment, but to draw from that the conclusion that the committee thought it was perfect or even a good idea is not a correct assumption. As a matter of fact the bill, although it is a short one and seems innocuous-because in effect all it does is to replace the three chiefs of staff with one chief of the defence forces, together with some consequential amendments-is a most important one. One might get the impression that because of the brevity of the bill it is not one of very great importance. Nothing could be further from the fact, because in the bill we are embarking on two principles as far as national defence is concerned, or we are perhaps embarking on one trend and continuing another which already exists in the National Defence Act.
The fact of the matter is that some members of the committee and numerous witnesses who appeared before the committee, such as Brigadier Malone and, speaking from memory, Air Marshall Curtis and some others, had very grave doubts about the wisdom of proceeding in this manner. In listening to the minister give evidence from time to time before the committee I could not help but get the feeling, and I do not say this in a critical sense, that there was a frightening naivete in that there seemed to be a subscription to the principle that progress is automatic, that all you have to do to achieve progress is to change things and if you change them it is progress. This, of course, is a very dangerous principle on which to proceed. We have to recognize that changes can be retrogressive as well as progressive, and that you do not just go blundering around changing things for the novelty of it, like some neurotic woman who is always changing the furniture in a room because it gives her a sense of relief or something. I have a feeling that there is a bit of this in the planning of the Department of National Defence.
As far as integration is concerned-and presumably this is the first step in this important matter-I think there is a lot that can be said in favour of it, although not for the replacement of the three armed services by one. I would violently oppose such a program. If we scrap our traditional three forces entirely and substitute therefore one force, perhaps with a green uniform or something of that sort, if we do away with all the traditions that have grown up over the years in
National Defence Act
the army, navy and air force, especially those army traditions that have grown up within the various units, if this first step we are now taking leads eventually to a program which will have that result, I think it will be a very unfortunate result.
However, the bill does not go that far. It only substitutes one chief of defence forces for the present three chiefs. But in this regard it can be looked upon as the first step in the direction of amalgamation of the three forces, or the replacement of the three forces with a new superforce, or perhaps just the co-ordination of the three forces, a knitting together more closely of the three forces by means of task forces made up of elements and personnel from all three of our forces for a particular duty. If the objective is the last name, I would support this trend fully; but if by starting on this road we end up by having one defence force, one uniform, no traditions and a complete obliteration of the marks of difference between the three forces that exist now, I would have very grave doubts about the wisdom of proceeding that way.
As I said when I commenced my remarks, the bill seems to be brief and to the casual observer a rather innocent sort of thing. It simply seeks to have one man replace three, which seems to be a good idea. But I was rather amazed at the minister's reasoning when he introduced the bill on second reading. He paid tribute to the Associate Minister of National Defence and said something to this effect, that if it had not been for the associate minister and all the work he had done in this connection it would have been impossible for the department to proceed as far as it had in certain directions. Then the minister proceeded to introduce a bill to replace three men with one. Following the same logic, the chief of the defence staff will be able to accomplish only one third as much as the three present chiefs of staff and half as much as the two national defence ministers.
He is going to have quite a job. From now on, we are going to have one chairman of the defence staff reporting to two ministers, whereas up to now we had at least three defence chiefs to keep two ministers occupied. One wonders, if this principle is followed, why it would not apply to the ministry itself. Why should we not combine the two portfolios into one, or perhaps even three portfolios? If you are combining the three chiefs of staff, why not combine the three ministers -the minister, the associate minister and the

National Defence Act
Minister of Defence Production-into one portfolio, or something of this sort, to eliminate waste and duplication? Presumably, this is the sort of thing we are doing in connection with the armed forces.
Then of course this procedure might run afoul of another government policy which was to divide some departments, such as the Department of Agriculture which, at one time, was to have a minister for the east and a minister for the west. Northern affairs might want to have a minister for the north and one for the south. We have a Department of National Defence with two ministers. I am not complaining about that fact. My remarks in this connection might sound a little facetious, but they are not intended to be. They are simply a test of this theory that by replacing three men with one you are going to effect economies. I do not believe it necessarily follows, because this one man may need far more men to help him in his immediate job than the three men put together required. The savings may not be as great as anticipated.
However, there is another and more important concept, so far as national defence is concerned, in relation to this bill. I want to talk about it for just a few minutes, Mr. Chairman. If one peruses statutes of Canada, he finds that there are fairly extensive acts setting up the various departments of government. Parliament has been quite specific in these acts in outlining the responsibilities of these departments and the various acts that are to be administered by them. In the case of the Department of National Defence, the National Defence Act is very brief so far as setting up the framework of the department is concerned. Practically all it does, in essence, is to appoint the chiefs of the various defence forces and set out some other main points of this type. Then, there is a great deal of detail with regard to non-public funds and matters of that sort, which really are not involved in setting out the framework of the department. However, the putting of the flesh on the bones, as it were, of the Department of National Defence is all done by orders in council, regulations, directives of the chiefs of staffs, and by some other means. There are no details set out in the National Defence Act that correspond to what is done in the acts of parliament which establish the various other departments of government and which give to the departments the various acts for which they are responsible. This leads me to a very grave problem which we fear this bill seems to ignore.

The government is consciously embarking on this type of policy and therefore it is the responsibility of the government. You can argue both sides of the case, as many witnesses did before the committee. You cannot therefore prove categorically that one thing is right and the other is not so good, or one will work under certain circumstances and not under others. The main question is this, whether parliament shall have, in effect, one individual, in this case the chief of the defence staff, who is going to be answerable to the minister for the defences of the country, or whether you are going to have a council, each member of which is appointed as a result of legislation and whose duties are specified in that legislation, so that he can be held responsible if a particular phase of defence is not up to par. There have been times in the past in British history when they had the chief of staff concept, that is total responsibility of a single individual rather than the committee system. Back in the last century, they found that there was grave danger in this system because inefficiency in the defence forces could grow up without parliament being advised sufficiently of the situation or without parliament being able to pin the responsibility on a particular individual.
In this system, the minister finds himself, in the last analysis, completely dependant on the advice of one man. If that man has particular theories as to what defence should be, it is only natural he will gather around him other senior officers who think in the same way as he does. He will then be in a position to have unanimity in the planning of the defence forces. If someone disagrees with him, he is only an adviser and can be replaced by someone who is more amenable to the points of view of the commander in chief concept which we have in this bill-one chief of the defence forces. As various witnesses pointed out in the committee, it is absolutely essential in a theatre of war, under wartime conditions, that the commander of the forces should have absolute control as to what he should do and that his orders cannot be questioned by a committee, countermanded at will, and so on. This is not a military operation. We are talking about the administration of a department of government which is set up to safeguard the country as best it can by having defence forces and administering them efficiently.
Now, how they operate in the field is a question for the military experts. This is not a question for civilians who are not trained

in that particular profession. But when it comes to the general question of administration, it seems to me the minister would be in a far sounder position if, as is the case in Britain, we had the committees system where the various members of the appropriate defence committee are responsible to the minister. I am using this term loosely, not in the technical sense. In Britain they have particular names for these committees, depending on whether they are for the navy, army or air force. There is the air force board, the army board and the admiralty board in the United Kingdom. In effect the members of a board are directly responsible to the minister and are not just in an advisory capacity to the chief of that particular branch of the armed services. In this way valid differences of opinion become known to the minister.
I want it clearly understood that it is not because of any lack of confidence in any particular individual that I have doubts about the system proposed. It is just because human nature being what it is nobody is perfect, and in my judgment when you have one man with total responsibility for large segments of the defence forces, and for policy, there is a certainty that, being human, he is going to make mistakes. Then there is a danger that these mistakes will not become known and recognized as quickly as they should be, because it is human nature to tend to defend one's position, whether it is right or not.
When you have this sort of set-up there is a danger that a bad decision will be defended for a long time, in fact until a great deal of damage has been done, and it will not become evident that there is a mistake until a lot of effort and possibly money has been wasted pursuing a particular course.
If we even had an inspector general of the defence forces, that would be an advantage, because then you would have the effectiveness of the forces under review by a technical expert who would be reporting directly to the minister on any flaws which his judgment told him existed in the armed forces. This would be a reasonable precaution. Otherwise the minister would be in the very difficult position in that his chief adviser on defence matters would be the man responsible for the shape, posture and condition of the defence forces. Under those circumstances weaknesses in the set-up would tend to be screened from the view of the minister, so long as it were possible to do so. In fact there might not even be a con-
National Defence Act
scious screening of dangers from the minister. These dangers might be pointed out to the chief of the defence forces but, because in his own mind he sincerely believes the forces are the best possible under the circumstances, he would inform the minister of his own view and the minister would not be made fully aware of other points of view.
I do not want to prolong this discussion. I have spoken longer than I expected to, but I just wanted to point out that members of the defence committee and witnesses who appeared before it raised grave doubts as to whether this is an improvement or a retrogression. Such doubts could be cured by having a defence council. There should be some latitude as to who the members of that council should be, but their positions would be specified by a bill, similar to this one, amending the National Defence Act. In fact this could be done, whether we had separate defence forces with three chiefs of staff or just one chief of staff. This is something that should be carefully examined by the government.
I, and many others far more expert than I would ever hope to be, have misgivings about this proposal. In other words many of us are not sure whether certain aspects of the bill are advancement or retrogression, in so far as efficiency of defence work in peacetime and the administration of it by the department are concerned. However, presumably on the best advice it could get, the government has embarked on this program. It is the government's responsibility to do that. All I can say is, heaven help it if it is a blunder.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, the position of our party in this connection was set out by the hon. member for Calgary North, when he said during the course of the committee hearings:
Mr. Chairman, I have really no further questions to put to the minister. I am not going to take up the time of the committee to repeat the points already made here, but I would like to say that I think that a lot of the points that Brigadier Malone brought up, which the minister has dealt with, chiefly in regard to the dangers of what amounts to a supreme commander, and particularly from the point of view of leaving the minister, whoever he may be, in the position of having only one military adviser, is a very dangerous precedent. It is a matter of going back, as Brigadier Malone pointed out, to a system which was tried for a long time in Great Britain and other countries and found wanting. I regret that the type of organization, more along the line of the one which exists in Great Britain or the type of thing which was suggested by Brigadier Malone, is not being put into effect.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I spoke at some length prior to this bill being sent to the special committee on defence, but there have been some points raised during the committee hearings that I feel I must underline once more.
As a member of the defence committee and on behalf of the official opposition I do say that while the principle of the unification of command is endorsed by us, yet we have some reservations about some of the consequences thereof. First I want to reiterate what my colleague, the hon. member for Queens, has said-and the minister knows my represensations and queries on this-that we are not satisfied the minister has the necessary framework of civilian advisers responsible to himself, rather than to the department.
Second, so long as we are talking about the unification of command, that is one thing; but there has been a great deal of loose talk about integration.
Frequently from the government we hear some odd predictions as to what may happen by July, 1967, without really thinking it out. I must warn the minister in this regard that there should be as full a disclosure as possible. Speed need not necessarily be the principal motive of the minister. I have had an opportunity during the last few weeks to talk to many of our servicemen and, let me assure the hon. gentlemen, there are a lot of questions in their minds. I do not know to whom in the armed services the minister has spoken. I know what happens when a minister visits a military establishment. He gets the official view, but no one dares to talk frankly from the lower levels. This is endemic in the system.
As a consequence of the reduction of personnel there were some 500 airmen selected for release recently. I believe we have seen headlines saying that 10 per cent of flight crews were to be released. This information may be reasonably accurate, or it may not. In any event I must say there is a great deal of dissatisfaction in the air force about what is happening in connection with these releases. I should like the minister to tell us what criteria were used to establish which men should be released. I have heard stories that young pilots whose careers were entirely ahead of them, men who had been trained at tremendous cost, are chiefly among those to be released. And where are they going? I am told many of them are going south of the border to obtain employment with United States air lines. I am informed that in training one unit where there were eight

instructors, seven of them have been slated for release. I would wish that this information were inaccurate, because if it is true it represents a monumental blunder to take seven eighths of a unit's training instructors and release them. What sort of efficiency results from a decision of that kind? If it is intended to release personnel from the army and the air force there are hundreds of jobs where men are piloting desks-jobs being done by men who are approaching the end of the road and serving their time before drawing their pensions. Those should be the men to be released at this time, rather than young men who have been trained and from whom we have so far received little return.
The minister may not know this, but actions of this type are seriously affecting morale. It may be true that within the junior ranks the prospect of integration is popular in certain sectors. However, I am speaking about these present releases. Actions now being taken have really shaken morale. I should like the minister, as I say, to give us some indication of the criteria being used to select personnel for release. Is it being done by using an IBM machine- certain cards being put into the machine, and out they come for release, those with certain qualifications or characteristics? We need some clarification of all these things; otherwise we can only be critical of the action of the department in selecting the personnel who are being released at this time. If the operation is carried out in this way in the air force, what is going to happen in the army? Is it the intention to take young officers who have been trained at high cost and from who we have received little in return, and release them, first?
I can assure the minister there are many other sectors within each of the services where the administrative set-ups could be combined. The recruiting services are an example. The practice on some occasions has been to take a pilot from overseas and put him in a recruiting office. Surely the department can do better than that. Surely you do not need an officer from each of the services to man a recruiting office. Take movement control of personnel; Every service has its own way of doing things. Pay is also handled differently. These, I suggest, are the areas in which real economies of personnel could be secured without a reduction in efficiency. The armed services are still fighting a considerable paper war, and the men employed in the services are the people who will tell you they are doing this.

Since I have spoken before, and since other members on this side of the house have made some inquiries of the minister, I think I will end my discussion of this item and bring it to a close.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think we should examine this bill which has come back to us from committee very carefully.
I am not suggesting the committee did not do an effective piece of work in examining the measure, but on reading over the evidence taken before that committee I express some disappointment that the subject was not covered in more detail.
The committee heard a statement from the minister and then listened to certain expert witnesses including Air Marshal Curtis and Major General Macklin. Officials of the Department of National Defence gave evidence also, and the committee heard a considerable statement from Brigadier Malone. But I do think the committee might usefully have made a study of the Lord Esher report which has been referred to on several occasions, as well as a study of the system now operating in the United Kingdom, and incorporated its findings on these two matters in the report.
As a matter of fact, I asked for this on May 8 as reported at page 3091 of Hansard. My words at that time were:
So I sound this cautionary note at this time for a consideration of the matters drawn to our attention by Brigadier Malone-
This refers to various articles he had written
-for a study of the Lord Esher report, for a study of the system operated at the present time in the United Kingdom, so that we do not, in the haste for reform, make what might become a very serious mistake.
That is the situation which faces us. Eagerness for reform should not lead the government or the House of Commons into an area of error, and I believe there is a chance for very serious error in the reform measure put before us in the present bill.
I realize that the minister has had a first class piece of public relations done on his efforts, and there has been the usual brainwashing with regard to his activities. People are led to believe that this is a major step forward and that something like this should have been done years ago. As my seatmate the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) has pointed out, it may turn out to be a major step backward because-and I said this on second reading of the bill-the minister is reverting to something which was in effect in Canada 60 years ago, something that was in effect in Britain 60 years ago, and it was changed in
National Defence Act
both places. Why is he reverting to something that was found faulty in those years. In the interval I do not doubt for one minute that certain discrepancies have crept in, not only here but in Great Britain, and adjustments have had to be made.
We have had the experience in Canada of the blunders that were made in the first world war, and they were numerous; and the blunders that were made in the second world war, and they were numerous. We also had a situation in Korea when we were not ready for that type of action and had to draw hastily from the militia units to throw up a force to dispatch to Korea; and when the 27th brigade was set up in Germany, we had to improvise and draw from various units in this country to provide a composite brigade for that operation. So I would say that although our experience in war has some worth-while aspects, we have committed as a country a great many blunders.
We should be very careful that we are not committing another blunder at the present time. That is why I think very careful consideration of the proposal of the minister is required. I would not be taking up the time of the house on this matter tonight were it not for the fact that I consider this step to be of very great seriousness. I do not profess to be an expert on warfare, but I have made a study of the conduct of war over the years and I am familiar with some of the problems that have faced governments in time of war, the difficulties of commanders in chief commanding in the field, and I have read quite a bit about the difficulties that have beset governments in dealing with the administration of defence departments in this country and in other countries.
So let us not just lightly rubber stamp this bill and say, "Oh, this is a very bright idea from a rising young star in the Liberal party", which is about what is said in the press releases which go out about the minister. He wants me to believe those press releases, but not the ones that pertain to the air division over in Europe, as he said today in the house. 1 am to believe the complimentary press releases. Let us not be in too great a haste about this matter.
What is the minister attempting to do? He talks, but has not explained this very clearly to the public and the services, about the unification or integration of the services. I think he should make clear in the house tonight exactly what is the situation in so far as the three services are concerned. I read in the committee report of Air Marshal

National Defence Act
Curtis talking to scores of officers, and he finds that in the services there is uncertainty as to what is happening. Surely, therefore, it is incumbent upon the minister to make a clear statement right here in the House of Commons so that the people in the services will know where they are going and what is ahead of them. Let him tell us whether we are going to have everybody in one type of uniform, all integrated together; or are we going to keep the three distinct fighting services and unify them in combined operations as was done in war, and leave it at that? Is his unification going to apply only to the administrative services, and that level? These are things that should be said, and said by the minister so that the responsible word can go out.
We do not want to lose able young men from the services, or able older men, just because of a scheme of integration which is not well understood. Why should men who have put many years into the services be now considering getting out in a hurry before some unknown change happens? The minister should give reassurance to these people who for years have been performing commendable service on behalf of their country. These are some of the uncertainties that should be cleared up, and cleared up now when we are discussing this bill which will set the pattern for future activity in this connection.
I mentioned the fact that I hoped the minister would have given us tonight a full report on the examination that the defence committee conducted with regard to this bill. The minister continually disappoints me. He gives a very short statement; he attempts to lull us into sleep, and we are to pass things just because everything is all right in this best of all worlds. Why did he not give us an exact, clear and comprehensive account of what transpired in that committee? He did not even mention the names of the expert witnesses. I noticed that when he was dealing with some of the statements made by Brigadier Malone, he brushed them aside. Brigadier Malone had made his presentation earlier to the committee, on about June 3, and on June 9 the minister offered his rebuttal. There is this interesting paragraph in the proceedings of the committee:
In commenting on what Brigadier Malone had to say, I think that in fairness to him I should point out that he himself admitted that, due to the fact that he had been out of the country recently, he had not been able to follow the proceedings of the committee prior to his appearance. Thus, he

was not aware of the discussions that had previously taken place, including my statement to the committee on May 26.
The inference there is that Brigadier Malone, having missed the statement from on high on May 26, was of course, not apprized of what really had been going on and was not competent then to offer criticism. I have read the statement that was made on May 26, and I cannot say that I learned much more, if anything, from it than what the minister had said when we debated this subject in the house. So the minister attempts to brush aside Brigadier Malone.
Let me point this out to the house, because the house has to take the responsibility; we do not foist this off on the defence committee. The house must know what it is about. It is the house that passes this bill after study by the committee; it is the house that has to make the decision. I find that there were three points of view presented to the committee by these three distinguished gentlemen who appeared there. Air Marshal Curtis, as I take it, did not like the idea of abolishing the heads of the three services. Major General Macklin was all for that change, and in his usual forceful and forthright manner he expressed his opinion on quite a number of subjects pertaining to defence, and one of them had to do with that. I have the greatest respect for Major General Macklin and have followed his career with a great deal of interest. I had the pleasure of working with him for a short interval toward the close of the war; I have followed his writings over the years with intense interest and have agreed, I think, with about 99 per cent of them. But 1 note that Major General Macklin had this to say with regard to the appointment of one person as supreme commander. As reported at page 210 of the committee report he said:
The whole thing depends upon the wisdom of the government in selecting the right chief. That means a man in whom they have confidence and who is qualified.
That is the nub of the matter, and this statement will apply to any government as the changes are made.
Now, what happens if the government selects the wrong chief? The system breaks down. This was the testimony that we got from Brigadier Malone, as he based it on the experience in England. I think from our knowledge of the first and second world wars we would say that that is where the danger lies. You do not always select the right man, and then trouble occurs between the minister of defence and the commander in chief. One

or the other has to give ground. We were not free from that in the second world war, when the government, I judge, was in a bit of a quandary for quite a while with regard to its commander in chief in the field before we invaded Europe. There was quite a little trouble in the first world war with a minister of national defence who caused endless concern to the people serving under him, and even more concern to his cabinet colleagues. So that getting the right man for the job is not easy.
As Brigadier Malone pointed out from the experience in Britain, that is where the trouble arises. You may have a very strong minister and a weak supreme commander. Or vice-versa; you have a very strong supreme commander and a weak minister, and you get into trouble. One or the other has to give way.
I should like to put on the record what Brigadier Malone said about this in his submission to the committee, as reported at page 146 of the report; and I would hope that the committee of the whole house would weigh some of this evidence. He said:
Assume for a moment that we could find a paragon of all the virtues to occupy the post of chief of the defence staff. In fact, a commander in chief. Look at the position in which he would be placed. All his professional associates would be junior to him, accepting his directions and orders and therefore not likely to challenge his decisions and no power to veto his projects. Above this one, top expert or professional soldier are the amateurs or civilians, in many cases not qualified or prepared to question his professional advice. It is hard to believe that such a top chief would not have some blind spots, some professional biases, some personal prides or fixations which would cause disaster. Surely the matter of national defence and the huge costs involved should not be subjected to such hazards. Certainly from an individual standpoint it is much easier to operate by yourself and be the complete boss and not have the problem worked through a committee, but it is not the individual interest we are thinking of here but the question of what is the right thing for the country.
The late Mr. Grant Dexter wrote on this subject back in 1942, and although Mr. Dexter and I disagreed on political matters I always respected the very able research that he put into any subject on which he wrote. This is what he wrote in 1942, and it is applicable to this particular case. He is speaking of the action taken in England in 1904:
The commander-in-chief was abolished for reasons which the Esher committee regarded as decisive. They were expressed by Mr. Balfour in the British house of commons and they apply to any minister who tries to control the army without the aid of an army council. To retain the commander-in-chief, said Mr. Balfour, meant that
National Defence Act
he would advise the secretary of state-then minister in Canada-and thereby the secretary must be destroyed. He would inevitably become only the nominal head-the puppet of the commander-inchief, the mouthpiece only. ...For a minister to deal directly with individual military experts is to place both minister and expert in a 'false position'. The minister must either confirm the expert's decision, in which case his position as superior authority is a mere form, or he must enter into the reasons for and against and decide afresh, in which case the expert becomes superfluous. It is bad organization to have two men (the minister and the expert), one over the other, to do the same business.
Brigadier Malone observed with regard to that:
It is my own conviction that the defence forces of Canada will be much more effectively directed by a defence council of both military and civilian personnel, rather than by a single officer directly under the minister. I would further suggest that each member of the defence council should be specifically charged by statute with clearly defined responsibilities. In my own opinion areas of actual responsibility are far too vague under our present system. I am convinced that these senior service members of the defence council should take their orders from the council as a whole not from a single commander-in-chief-or chief of the defence staff-call him what you will.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the nub of the matter. Do you have one supreme commander, or do you have a defence council which gives instructions to that commander?

speechtext:
It was the submission of Brigadier Malone immediately after he had read the comment made by Grant Dexter.
The minister attempted to answer some of the questions which Brigadier Malone put in front of him when he made his submission to the committee on defence, and I should now like to bring the minister back into the picture again. As reported at page 212 he said:
I would like, therefore, to take each of these questions in turn.
These are the questions put forward by Brigadier Malone.
The first: "Will the proposed chief of defence staff be accepting orders, directions and decisions from the defence council, or will he, in fact, be imposing his decisions on this council?"
The ministers goes on as follows:
The answer to this is that the chief of the defence staff will be accepting orders from the

National Defence Act
minister and associate minister. These orders will be based on decisions taken following full discussion within the defence council.
So here you have two men, the minister and the chief of the defence staff, and the chief takes his orders directly from the minister. The minister may not know anything about defence.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does this one?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What position does this put the chief of the defence staff in? I continue quoting:
His second question was: "Will other members of the defence council be in a position to question him or overrule him or veto his decisions?"
The minister replied:
The defence council will be the senior policy making group within the Department of National Defence under the chairmanship of the minister and all members of the defence council will be perfectly free at all times to ask any questions they so desire and to express their opinions on any subject which is before the council.
He did not answer the question except in part. The question was: Will they be able to overrule him or veto his decisions? The minister simply says that they can express their opinions on any subject which is before the council. That is what he says to us here: You can express your opinions on any subject with regard to defence. I recall that when I asked him last year in the defence committee if he wanted the advice of that committee he said "no". We sat for week after week knowing that the minister did not really want our advice. He does not want mine tonight, but I am giving it to him.
The third question was: "Will other members of the defence council be junior and subordinate to him?"
To the chief of the defence staff. The minister replied:
The answer to this is...that the membership of the council will consist of the minister, the associate minister, the ministers' parliamentary secretaries, if applicable, the chief of the defence staff, the vice-chief of the defence staff, the deputy minister and the chairman of the defence research board. Of these, only the vice-chief of defence staff can be considered subordinate to the chief.
Then there are some other questions which I do not think I will go into at this time, with the exception of this one:
"Will the chief of the defence staff be the chief adviser to the minister? Officially, will other members of the defence council have to speak to the minister through him?"
This was the minister's answer:
The answer to the first part of the question is that the chief of the defence staff will be the senior military adviser to the minister. To the

second part, other members of the defence council will speak in the defence council directly to the minister, if required, and...both the deputy minister and the chairman of the defence research board will have direct access to the minister at all times.
Another question asked by Brigadier Malone was:
"Will the actual authority for carrying out the government's policies as directed by the minister be vested in the council or in the chief of the defence staff?
This is the crux of the matter. The minister replied:
The answer to that is that the policies of the government will be carried out by several members of defence council in accordance with their responsibilities.
That is not very clear. I think what the minister is aiming at is having a supreme chief of the defence staff to whom he will give his orders, and that chief will give his orders down the line. The council that the minister talks about will just be an advisory council, free to express their opinions on any subject under the sun but having no authority to give instructions. In my opinion this is the point at which the mistake is being made.
According to the experience we had in this country many years ago and the experience in Great Britain, and both countries have had experience of war, there is an advantage in having a council which takes the responsibility and transmits its orders to the chief of staff rather than having him as a supreme commander. It is not only a question of limited aspects of the service. The council, if it had full authority, in addition to surveying all the aspects of military service would be able to give instructions so that there would be a proper balance in our services. The function of our armed services is to be ready for war in case of emergency and the council should be prepared to give the necessary instructions, with the minister being answerable to parliament for the activities of that council of which he would be a member. But if the bill of the minister is accepted we will have the minister still responsible to parliament for activities within defence, but there will be one man and one man only who will carry the responsibilities one step further. If there is a conflict of interest somebody will have to go, either the minister or the chief of the defence staff.
This is the danger inherent in the bill before us and it should be guarded against. Some may say: The man we have in mind for the chief of the defence staff right now

is a very able man, and I express no doubt on that score whatsoever. Perhaps his successor will be too, and maybe his successor; but a bill of this nature is long term, long range planning. Ministers come and go and sometimes there will be an experienced minister and sometimes an inexperienced minister. If there is an inexperienced minister or a minister who during the course of his functions in that job is detracted by other pressing problems, or suffers temporary illness or something of that nature, the supreme commander gains even more power.
Therefore when we make such long range plans we should be extraordinarily careful about what we are doing. The minister has not yet pointed out to the house in what way his plan is superior to the one put before the house by some of us on this side, when we spoke earlier in the debate, and put before the committee on defence by Brigadier Malone. Let the minister tell us the weaknesses, if there are any, of Brigadier Malone's submission and the corresponding strength, if there is any, of his proposal because, as I say, this is a very serious matter indeed and it will have its effect in the future.
We have no idea, and in my lifetime we never have had in this country, when war will break out, or where, or the contribution that Canada will be called upon to make. We have fooled ourselves all through the 20th century. We are very peaceful people, we are not going to participate in war, and all of a sudden we do. Then we find ourselves unprepared for it. Let us profit from the mistakes of the past and make sure that in the proposed reform that is before us now we are doing the right thing. If this is the right thing to do, why was it discontinued in 1904 in Canada and in Great Britain? Why has it not been reverted to in Great Britain? These are the questions I should like the minister to answer.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have before us Bill No. C-90, an act to amend the National Defence Act. I have read the debates of May 8, 11 and 12 and I was in the house at the time. I have had an opportunity to examine the proceedings of the defence committee, and I feel that as a committee of the whole house we have a very definite duty to go into the bill most thoroughly and also into defence policy generally. There has been enough material brought before the house to show that there is a very strong difference of opinion. Many points were raised by the last two speakers and all of them were good. I
National Defence Act
would only add to them the speech made by the hon. member for Calgary North during the debate early in May.
A lot of questions were asked of the minister, I don't know, but he seems to see all and hear all, and he speaks damn all when he gets on his feet. I think this is something that he should take to heart. These questions are not put to him to put him on the spot. We are all interested in the defence of this country. We are interested in the defence policy of the present government. We are interested in expenditures. We are interested in how far we are going and not in an airy-fairy ten year plan without a fuller explanation.
The minister referred to his white paper and said that sometimes-I have not got his exact words here-there has been too much criticism; it is too detailed. I put it to him now that there is a happy medium. In other words, he can say something after hearing all and seeing all. I have no doubt the minister, in his capacity as minister and a member of the cabinet, has many things put to him. There are considerations and great ponderings going on, but some of these things must seep down. We are not getting it in this house. Naturally, this bill does not cover all these things, but I do think we are entitled to get at these things.
If I understood the associate minister today when he was asked if he had heard any complaints about the cutting down of the armed forces, he said, "Not to my knowledge." Perhaps the minister heard that statement. I ask the minister now, has he heard any complaints, general or specific, from specific people? Has he had any complaints from those who are under him in the armed services in the highest capacity, people upon whom he must rely? What have they told him? We heard the hon. member for Edmonton West ask about the reductions in the armed services. The questions he asked were good ones because I have heard them myself from members of the armed services. He mentioned air crew and members of the air force. I have heard this complaint myself. I should like the minister to tell us how he went about these reductions. The member for Edmonton West made a very excellent speech about these people.
We undertook a very heavy recruiting campaign on which we spent a lot of money to obtain these people. They received their university education along general lines, and then we find there is a terrific cutting off of these men who have come into Canada's

National Defence Act
armed forces with the intention of making it a career. Were these men cut off simply- I see the minister shaking his head, so I imagine now we are going to get the policy in connection with these cut-backs.

speechtext: He has no policy.

speechtext:
I think he may have. We are entitled to know whether that is a good policy, and where he got it from. Was it a slide rule deal? Was it an ivory tower deal? How was it arrived at? Some of these young men are married and they have devoted their lives to the particular branch of the armed services to which they belong.
I was speaking about the air force. The training of air crew members, apart from their academic training, is fantastically detailed and very expensive to this country. The member for Edmonton West asked about these desk-bound boys. What was the proportion of these men amongst those who were discharged, or whose discharges are pending? Are we clipping off too many of these air force people who have that detailed knowledge? Are we retaining a great many ivory tower people who probably have greater seniority? I agree with the point made by the hon. member for Edmonton West. He said we had trained these men and they will be needed in our armed forces.
I have gone into this matter in considerable detail. Unless we do get answers from the minister, I think we are entitled to come back and back and back until we do get answers commensurate with reason. The minister gave a slight dissertation on May 12 which is reported in Hansard. I have read that speech several times and I ask myself, what did he say other than the broadest generalities? We have in this bill the big chief concept which has been gone into so thoroughly by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. He is quite right. You put everything in one basket and things can happen. I think the remarks he made deserve a thorough answer from the minister. I should like to have an answer myself because I had notes on this subject. I wanted to know why we were going to this one chief idea, when so much criticism has been levelled against it down through the history of armed forces, not only here but elsewhere in the world.
There is no doubt that the Minister of National Defence has made a thorough study of this subject, but we do not have the benefit of his study. I think we are entitled to it. I like that point; who takes orders from whom? I can see the minister, if something did occur

which would require his sterling advice on military matters, based on his long background as a military man, arguing with his one chief. Perhaps there would not be an argument because I know the minister fairly well. I can see him pointing his finger at that chief and saying, "You do this". He might be wrong. As one hon. member remarked in referring to the C.B.C., heads will roll. When you get into trouble, heads cannot roll. We have had troubles before. We had a build-up in the armed services on the basis of seniority, and in the last war we had tremendous trouble from policy to actuality. The minister knows that because I am sure, in his capacity as Minister of National Defence, he has studied that situation and studied it carefully.
Then, I am wondering about the Glassco commission and how far it has gone. If we take the minister's word, then I suppose it is part of the ten year plan. The hon. member for Calgary North referred to this and asked what the recommendations of the Glassco commission were. The minister said that, apart from the integration of the forces and increased responsibility to the deputy minister, as outlined in the white paper, many of these recommendations were, in fact, now being implemented. I believe this committee is entitled to know how far you are going to go. What is the policy? What is the objective? What are the total military objectives? How are you going to accomplish them, bearing in mind the questions of equipment, material, manpower and the amount of money we can spend on these things We have not had that. It is sort of like this flexible deal. You go back to it many times and you say, "keep her flexible". How flexible have you got to be?
I go back again to that one instance, the chopping of men and personnel in the armed forces, and the breakdown of morale. I cannot use any other word because that is exactly what has happened. We should know what is going on; we should know how far we are going.
The minister smiles, because I think he has thought of the answer. He is going to say, "Well, you know there are a lot of things I would love to tell you boys about, but I am sorry they are locked away in the secret files and they must remain there." But I do not think he has given us enough. In common sense, I don't think he has given us enough.
We read too much in the newspapers; too many little kites are being flown. We should

have these things put before us in an orderly fashion, so that if there are any areas which the minister cannot delineate he should tell us about them and perhaps, within reason, we would say, "Well, all right."
I go back to the minister's reaction when he was in opposition, when he was a hard working, intermediate backbencher, though possibly on the front bench of the opposition. Now that we are in opposition we want to know more, and if there is an explanation which falls short of what is expected, then we should keep the ball rolling and say, "I don't understand that answer. We should know more." I know the minister knows exactly what I am referring to because these were supplementary estimates which galloped on for the longest time in history and a good deal of the verbiage in Hansard was produced by the clack of the present minister, who was the great defence man for the opposition at that time.
He was a critical critic. I think I have put my point across and I would repeat what I said at the outset, that this a committee of the whole house. The minister had his say in the defence committee. He may or may not have answered the questions to our satisfaction, but the hon. member for Edmonton West said there were reservations, and if that hon. member has reservations I am sure they are just. I think we should hear further. I do not think he is the type of man who wants to prod and pry and unleash vital information, like a regular Mata Hari deal. We are making a common sense demand and we are entitled to have the answers because this committee, in the final analysis, is going to pass not only Bill C-90, but also the minister's estimates and the various other productions which he is going to present from now until such time as he is elevated, removed or moved out. But so long as he is sitting there we are going to have these things put before us, and in a great deal more detail.

I am glad to see I have support from the other side because it helps the morale to find such enlightened people among others, as the hon. member for Vancouver Quandra, a distinguished member of the committee, approving in advance what I may say on this measure.
So far as integration is concerned, I think we on this side have amply manifested that
National Defence Act
we are in accord with the principle of integration of the forces, and that is the natural outcome of the vast changes which have taken place in military technology in the post-war years. The roles of the traditional services can no longer be clearly defined and they overlap one another. In view of that development it is only natural that we should use ways to bring the organization of the forces in line with it.
But I think this bill has been greatly overrated and promoted out of all proportion by the minister, his worthy associate and everyone else connected with it. I remember the minister telling the committee that Bill C-90 would make our armed forces the most modern anywhere in the world, but if you ask him how he substantiates such a sweeping statement all he says is, "We are bringing forth an act to amend national defence administration."
If you closely analyse this bill you find there is only one substantive disposition in all of it, clause No. 1, which relates to section 19 of the act, and which refers to the appointment of a chief of the defence staff who will be replacing the present three chiefs of service. There is nothing very revolutionary in such a proposal, and by integrating the chiefs of staff this does not mean we are creating, to use his own words, the most modern force in the world. I notice the minister laughing, and also his associate minister. They think this matter is very funny-and it may be; but in any event this measure in itself does not improve the effectiveness of the forces, nor does it effect any real economy in military spending.
I ask the minister if he can prove that this is not so?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is not.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The minister says it is not so, but he did say in the committee that the purpose of the bill was twofold-one, to make the forces more effective and, second, to realize economies in military spending. With regard to making the forces more effective and modern, all we have here is a proposal to appoint this chief of the defence staff who will be reporting direct to the minister, and in the eyes of the minister this is performing a great revolutionary modification to our armed forces. He thinks our forces will be

National Defence Act
a lot more modern because they will be under one chief of general staff, instead of under three persons.
You might well have some kind of an armed force belonging to a very backward country east or west or south of Timbuktu, a newly emerging nation, but all it has are a couple of soldiers with bow and arrows, and these are all placed under one man. But from the fact that these people have been placed under one commander, instead of three, I ask: Does that make them any more modern? The minister may think this comparison has no application to the present case; but it has a direct application. All we are doing here is integration by the top instead of by the bottom, down below. Integration in such a way is simply integration on paper; that is all the minister has so far performed.
I know the minister has a good publicity staff. His public relations are excellent. No doubt they are warranted. He is an amiable man. He knows how to make friends and influence people. He has probably read all the right books on the subject and I think perhaps in this respect the minister is the most successful the country has ever had. In this respect, that is so, but in this respect only-on paper, and as far as spreading the aura of renovation across the country. I myself had the privilege of travelling with the minister a few weeks ago and I had an enjoyable trip. To give an example-I do not think he will hold it against me if I bring this up-to show how well he likes to have his colleagues and other people know in what high regard he is held-and I think he is held in high regard-he distributed in the plane some copies of the Armed Forces Management Review, a United States publication which is supposed to be directed to executives in military affairs, and on the front cover of that magazine was a splendid picture, not flattering at all-the minister is an impressive looking gentleman-and I went on to read the review because, naturally, I was attracted by the presentation. The minister was described as "the boy wonder of Canadian politics". I think that is really treating public relations in the proper fashion. I think some of us could learn a few things about the way these things are carried on.
But the crux of the matter is that the only reason for the minister being described as the boy wonder of Canadian politics, and doing things which have never been done

before in western military history, is that he has introduced this bill to amend the National Defence Act. That is all very well, and I wish the minister a lot of success with this venture; but I think that we on this side of the house are genuinely concerned about the effectiveness of these changes. If integration is a good principle-and we agree it is a good principle-it should be carried on right down the line, and so far we have not had very much proof that what the minister is proposing is either going to increase effectiveness or realize economies.
For instance, this replacement of the chiefs of the services by one chief of a defence staff may appear to represent a reduction from three to one, but this is not necessarily so because the new chief will have a number of assistants. He will have an assistant from each of the services and there will be, of course, if this tendency toward empire building takes its usual course, a desire on the part of each of those senior staff, the top brass of the Canadian forces, to be surrounded by aides-de-camp and all the staff which surrounds senior brass in any armed service in any country in the world-a tendency from which Canada has shown no marked willingness to escape.
So it would seem that the second object will not be realized; and if, as I fear, the human tendency to empire building as exemplified in Parkinson's law applies, we will see just as much brass as we ever had in the armed forces of Canada. The minister may think that because only one person will be reporting to him it will be a significant change for the better, but I am not so sure. The hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean), the hon. member for Winnipeg South and a number of others mentioned that it is better to get information from a variety of sources, as the minister knows very well, so as to possess a broader picture of the real needs of Canadian defence.
Someone else has pointed out that this great project of the minister has stirred up a lot of talk among the people of this country and especially among service people. Members of the armed forces are entitled to get from the minister a clearcut picture of what is actually to happen to them. These men are fine, trained men and they have devoted their best years to the service of Canada. They have not yet received a clear picture of what the minister has in mind. They could not have received one because we in this committee have not yet received from the minister any clear picture apart from this one enactment.

So before this bill goes further I think the minister should answer a number of questions pertaining to the changes he may have in mind. How is this integration to be followed up by integration among the lower ranks of the armed services? I know the department intended to release at one stage some 50,000 men from the armed services. The next day it was 10,000. Then in committee several members questioned the minister and the associate minister very closely about the number of men who were to be released. The numbers seemed to get smaller and smaller until, in the end, I was not sure whether instead of decreasing the armed forces we were not planning to increase them. It was clear that only a puny operation was contemplated under the smokescreen of this vast renovation which was to produce for Canada a great force of armed might whose efficiency no other nation could approach. That is certainly a worthy objective to be pursued, but so far we have not seen the beginning of it, despite this barrage of publicity which accompanies the merest gesture the minister makes. I do not know what his secret is, but he is certainly in the foreground of public speculation and, perhaps, even of adulation; I do not know. But I think the armed services are a bit worried. They want to know what is likely to happen to them, and those who are to be released wish to be treated on a fair and equitable basis.
It is all right to provide for colonels or major generals up to $15,000 in cash benefits. That is fine. The associate minister said in the committee that the purpose of these benefits was simply to help in the rehabilitation of those who were released. Yet those who are in the greatest need of help for rehabilitation, that is to say the lower ranks, the private soldiers without any great influence or special skills, get very much less. This is a line of policy from which neither the minister nor the associate minister wanted to depart one iota.
I mentioned this in the committee, and afterwards I received a lot of letters from people in the armed services. They feel it is unfair-and I do, too, in a way. If the purpose is really to provide rehabilitation, I do not think the private should get five, six or ten times less than the major general. I just cannot accept the particular explanation given by the minister in this regard, and I do not think this practice is fair.
These are matters that are directly concerned with this bill, Mr. Chairman, and with regard to which we have not received the
National Defence Act
answers that we should receive from the minister. We asked in the committee what would be the role of this new, integrated force Canada will have, and the minister said, "Well, read the white paper". That is all he could tell us. I have read the white paper- and I have here a very good summary of the principal points contained in the white paper-but it only deals in generalities. These generalities, in order to be meaningful, must be accompanied by positive actions and statements by the minister. I would like the minister to tell the committee now what the next step in this integration will be; and let him tell us what the new role of the armed forces will be once this integration has been completed. If he can do that, I think the minister will finally deserve all the advance publicity, all the advance favourable notice he has received about the things he intends to do but has not yet done. I think it is about time this government found out there is a vast distinction between saying they are going to do something, and doing it.
The press have treated the minister and his work most favourably. I do not think there is a single minister of the present government, with the possible exception of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has been so well treated by the press. If this is so, it is because they expect many things from the minister-and so far he has not delivered. If his delivery is nothing but the very insignificant changes that are being wrought by this bill, I think it is about time he changed his tune and admitted that what he proposed to do is just a little bit too much for him, and that he will call upon other advisers if necessary to carry out this job. This is very important. The minister has started on a course, and for my part I am glad to see him start on that course and I want to congratulate him; but I want him to continue and I want him to be frank, and perfectly frank, with all the members of this committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIABILITY OF CORPORATION AND EXPORTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-101, to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in view of the late hour I wish to try and summarize my remarks on this bill. As hon. members know, the Export Credits Insurance Act was originally approved in 1944. It has been amended from time to time over the years to enable the Export Credits Insurance Corporation to provide facilities in line with current demands. This bill marks another stage in the development of the corporation's activities.
One purpose of the present bill is to exempt the corporation from the obligation of paying income tax. No similar export credits insurer doing business in other countries along the same lines as the Export Credits Insurance Corporation pays income tax. In addition, there are no commercial enterprises in Canada providing services comparable to the facilities provided by the Export Credits Insurance Corporation. If this amendment is approved by parliament it is proposed that under the provisions of the Financial Administration Act the corporation will pay to the Receiver General the sum of $10 million in cash. This sum corresponds to the aggregate of the paid-up capital and the capital surplus of the corporation and will be credited to a special non-interest bearing account in the consolidated revenue fund in the name of the corporation.
Another main purpose of the bill relates to the corporation's authority to insure Canadian engineering and construction firms for services rendered overseas. In this field of export operation, particularly with respect to construction, certain equipment must be taken to the site and would normally be brought back to Canada on completion of the job. The purpose of the proposed amendment is to permit the corporation to insure the Canadian firm against the risk of losing the ownership or control of the equipment being employed by him in rendering technical services outside Canada. Such insurance is not at present available from commercial sources.

Export Credits Insurance Act
The bill would also give the corporation authority to reinsure risks with export credits insurers operating in other countries and to accept reinsurance from them, thus providing the corporation with the authority to take on additional insurable business of Canadian exporters. The corporation can now enter into a contract of insurance with a Canadian exporter to protect him against non-payment by a foreign buyer for goods or services exported from Canada pursuant to a contract of sale entered into between the Canadian exporter and the foreign buyer. With the proposed amendment it will be possible for the corporation to enter into a contract of insurance with an export credits insurance organization in another country.
The bill proposes to increase the amount of the liability of the corporation under contracts of insurance entered into under section 21 of the act from $400 million to $600 million. Under this section, the total current liability of the corporation as at April 30 this year under all policies issued and outstanding amounts to $235 million. Additional commitments have been made under the authority of orders in council totalling $236 million. So it will be quite clear to the house that we need this authority if we are going to continue doing business.
Section 21A of the Export Credits Insurance Act allows the corporation, when authorized by the governor in council by order in council, to provide financing to Canadian exporters for heavy capital equipment requiring terms of payment extending beyond five years, which is the normal cut-off term for insurance transactions. This bill proposes to increase the amount of this long term financing from the present limitation of $300 million to $400 million. As at April 30 of this year the corporation had entered into financial agreements under long term export financing contracts totalling $184 million. Additional financing and guarantees have been authorized by orders in council totalling $33 million. The corporation has applications from exporters for long term financing, the bulk of which has been approved in principle, totalling another $80 million. Accordingly, financial agreements already signed, guarantees currently outstanding, and additional financial agreements not yet signed total $297 million. It is therefore obvious that in order to continue this very important facility it is necessary to increase the present ceiling.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has referred


to the various technical amendments which are included in this bill, all of which I am sure are important. I think the crux of the bill is contained in the last paragraphs of his statement with reference to sections 20, 21, and 21 A, under which obviously unless this bill is passed, and passed in the immediate future, there would be a severe curtailment of the financing of exports which are necessary to maintain the development of this country.
I have always been interested in this matter first, as minister of national revenue and afterwards as minister of finance, and I felt sometimes that our act was not as generous as those of other countries. I am thinking of the excellent arrangements made in the United States. I am thinking of the way export credit insurance matters are dealt with in other nations. I realize the difficulties of the signatories to the Berne convention. I was reminded of that from time to time by the chairman of the corporation. I was trying to persuade him to accept some long term arrangements and he said: "We are a signatory to the Berne convention and we can do nothing about it".
I am glad to see that these amendments are being suggested and I am particularly happy to see the increase in the capital and the increase in the authorization under section 21 A. This has been one of the keystones of our economic development. The government of which I was a member amended the act on two or three occasions, increasing the moneys which were available, and it is an indication of the development of the export trade of Canada that it is now necessary and advisable for the minister to come before us to ask for a further extension. As far as we in the official opposition are concerned, we are very glad to give our full support to the proposed amendments, and I hope they commend themselves to the favourable attention of the house because I am quite certain they are necessary now and in the immediate future.

INCOME TAX-QUEBEC  FEDERAL REFUNDS MADE TO PROVINCIAL MINISTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to congratulate the minister upon his elevation to the cabinet. I think all of us will agree, although on occasion we do not agree with his philosophy on the principles of taxation, he has already demonstrated his ability to deal with exactitude with figures when he has been answering questions by the opposition about legislation or estimates. It is in that co-operative spirit, Mr. Speaker, that I provide this opportunity for the minister to get his initiation into the details of the administration of the Income Tax Act.
I should like to quote the question I asked him on orders of the day today. Would the minister inform the house why the income tax branch forwards refunds due residents of Quebec to the provincial ministry of revenue direct, and of the legal basis for such unusual procedure? My reason for asking that question follows a conversation I had yesterday with some Quebec residents. In one instance in particular-and the person had the document with him to prove it-the refund of something like $60 which this person fully expected to receive was sent to the provincial department of revenue. The taxpayer in question received a notice from the income tax branch that the refund payable to the taxpayer was being paid to the provincial department of revenue.
This procedure caused the taxpayer in question, and some others who had a similar experience, to consider it a very high-handed procedure, almost an invasion of the privacy of the individual. They were quite indignant. I should like, therefore, to fulfil my function as a member of parliament by raising this

question at the first opportunity. I brought it up during the question period and was disappointed when the Speaker said I was not in order. I thought this was a question of fiscal policy that concerned the whole house and would concern the country.
I would like the minister to explain to the house the arrangements that have been made in this connection, and the procedure and legal basis for this type of action on the part of the income tax branch. Also, would he mind informing the house when this procedure was first adopted. Is it part of a recent fiscal arrangement with the province of Quebec, or has it lasted for some time?
We are all interested in not only, shall I say, the immediate question of what appears to be a very high-handed procedure in sending money coming to someone to another government, but also in the sort of behind-the-scenes events that may have transpired to produce this, what appears at the moment, somewhat unusual regulation and procedure.

Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), I thought today during question period I could be an ideal Minister of National Revenue in that I was simply able to answer "no" to the two questions raised in the house, and I am sure over the period in which I

However, to deal specifically with this question, under the reciprocal arrangements between the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec, a person who has been employed in Ontario during a year and was resident in Quebec on the last day of that year does not receive a refund from the federal government for the tax deductions made in Ontario, but he does receive credit for the amount of such deductions on his Quebec income tax return.
As everyone will recall, the province of Quebec collects its own provincial income tax. Similar arrangements apply where a person was employed in Quebec during the year and was resident in Ontario on the last day of the year. The authority for this procedure is found in the Ontario income tax act and the Quebec income tax act. The Department of National Revenue, taxation division, is acting in these cases as the agent of the province of Ontario to carry out these arrangements under the general authority of the tax collection agreement.
The hon. member asked me the exact date of the passing of the approval of this tax collection agreement. I do not happen to have this available at the moment, but I shall be pleased to tell him within the next day or so.
